---

#### TEAM & PHILOSOPHY

- **Author of launch post:** Sundar Pichai (SVP, Android, Chrome & Apps in 2014).
  - Source: [blog.google — An inbox that works for you](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gmail/an-inbox-that-works-for-you/) (HIGH confidence)

- **Product lead:** Alex Gawley, Director of Product Management for Gmail, headed up development of Inbox. He joined Google in 2006 as a financial analyst, moved to PM, and by 2008 led Gmail and Calendar.
  - Source: [Business Insider India — Alex Gawley profile](https://www.businessinsider.in/rising-stars-meeting-the-men-and-women-leading-some-of-googles-most-important-products/Alex-Gawley-director-of-product-management-for-Gmail-and-Calendar/slideshow/46519794.cms) (MEDIUM confidence — profile, not primary launch doc)

- **Lead designer:** Jason Cornwell (Google's lead designer for Inbox by Gmail, confirmed as leading designer for both Gmail and Inbox). Demonstrated the app at a media preview in New York on October 29, 2014.
  - Source: [Getty Images caption](https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/googles-lead-designer-for-inbox-by-gmail-jason-cornwell-news-photo/458046608); [Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/person/jason-cornwell) (MEDIUM confidence for title)
  - Source: [Android Police AMA recap — Gmail Team's Inbox AMA](https://www.androidpolice.com/2014/12/03/catch-gmail-teams-inbox-ama-answers-questions-functionality-future-plans/) (AMA participants were Vijay U [PM], Jason C [Designer], Taylor K [Engineer])

- **Jacob Bank:** Co-founder/CEO of Timeful (a time-management app), acquired by Google in May 2015. Timeful's technology was integrated into Inbox, Calendar, and Gmail. Bank became Director of PM at Google for Gmail, Hangouts Chat, and Google Groups after the acquisition. He was not part of the original Inbox founding team.
  - Source: [SiliconAngle — Google acquires Timeful](https://siliconangle.com/2015/05/05/google-acquires-timeful-to-bring-you-a-smarter-calendar/)
  - Source: [Crunchbase — Jacob Bank](https://www.crunchbase.com/person/jacob-bank)

- **Matthew Izatt:** Identified as Gmail product manager who gave the official shutdown quote: "Inbox by Gmail has been a great place to experiment with new ideas like snoozing emails to later, as well as try the latest AI-powered experiences like Smart Reply, Nudges and high-priority notifications..."
  - Source: [Fortune — Google to Kill Its Inbox App In Favor of Gmail](https://fortune.com/2018/09/12/google-inbox-gmail-email/)

- **Stated design philosophy (from the original launch post, confirmed via defuddle):**
  - "it's not Gmail: it's a completely different type of inbox, designed to focus on what really matters"
  - "For many of us, dealing with email has become a daily chore that distracts from what we really need to do—rather than helping us get those things done."
  - "your inbox becomes a centralized place to keep track of the things you need to get back to"
  - Closing line: "It's a better way to get back to what matters"
  - The underlying thesis was that the inbox should function like a to-do list and an assistant, not a message archive. Cornwell framed this as: "kind of like an assistant putting your mail into piles to make it easier to deal with."
  - Source: [blog.google — An inbox that works for you](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gmail/an-inbox-that-works-for-you/) (PRIMARY, HIGH confidence)
  - Source: [Washington Post — Inbox: A new, simpler approach](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/inbox-a-new-simpler-approach-for-your-gmail/2014/11/07/5eb88828-6470-11e4-9fdc-d43b053ecb4d_story.html) (Cornwell quote)

- **Why built as a separate product (from Cornwell in AMA, December 2014):** "we didn't feel like we could solve those problems by just adding more features on to Gmail." Long-term goal: "we hope that everyone will want to use Inbox instead of Gmail."
  - Source: [Android Police AMA recap](https://www.androidpolice.com/2014/12/03/catch-gmail-teams-inbox-ama-answers-questions-functionality-future-plans/) (MEDIUM-HIGH confidence)

- **Material Design:** Inbox was built on Material Design principles. The AMA designer (Jason C) noted the "Material Design guidelines were still under development while many recent apps were being designed," meaning Inbox was built somewhat concurrently with Material Design itself.
  - Source: [Android Police AMA](https://www.androidpolice.com/2014/12/03/catch-gmail-teams-inbox-ama-answers-questions-functionality-future-plans/)

---

#### PLATFORM DIFFERENCES

- **Mobile-first design:** Inbox launched simultaneously on web (inbox.google.com), Android, and iOS — but was explicitly designed mobile-first. Swipe gestures (left to snooze, right to archive/done) were core UX rather than a mobile adaptation. The blue header vs. Gmail's red was a deliberate design distinction.
  - Source: [Android Authority — The new Gmail vs Inbox differences explained](https://www.androidauthority.com/gmail-vs-inbox-881961/)
  - Source: [Computerworld — Gmail vs. Inbox: 8 features Gmail still can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

- **Smart Reply: mobile-only at launch (Nov 2015), web added March 2016.** This is the clearest documented case of a feature being mobile-first then expanded to web.
  - Source: [9to5Google — Inbox by Gmail adds Smart Reply suggestions for web users](https://9to5google.com/2016/03/15/inbox-gmail-smart-reply-suggestions-web/) (HIGH confidence)

- **Inline attachment previews:** Inbox showed attachment thumbnails under each email in the list view on both mobile and web. The Gmail Android app at the time did not have this; Gmail web did. This made mobile Inbox closer to Gmail web than Gmail mobile in this respect.
  - Source: [Android Authority — Gmail vs Inbox](https://www.androidauthority.com/gmail-vs-inbox-881961/)

- **"Save to Inbox" / web link saving:** Required the Inbox Chrome extension on desktop web; on mobile it used the OS share sheet. This was an intentional mobile-first workflow.
  - Source: [Computerworld — 8 features Gmail can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

- **Swipe-to-snooze and swipe-to-done:** Core to mobile experience. Inbox's swipe philosophy replaced the Gmail swipe-to-archive with a snooze/done model. On web, similar actions were available via hover buttons and keyboard shortcuts.
  - Source: [Computerworld — 8 features Gmail can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

- **Bundle sweeping:** On mobile, swiping up on a bundle or tapping the sweep icon dismissed all its messages at once. Could also pin individual messages before sweeping the rest. Available on both mobile and web but optimized for mobile gesture.
  - Source: [Computerworld — 8 features Gmail can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

- **iOS noted as better than Gmail's own iOS app at launch.** David Pierce (The Verge): Inbox was "far better on iOS than the Gmail app."
  - Source: [Wikipedia — Inbox by Gmail (quoting The Verge review)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbox_by_Gmail)

- **"Canned responses" (text templates):** Available on desktop web only, not in mobile apps.
  - Source: [Android Authority — Gmail vs Inbox](https://www.androidauthority.com/gmail-vs-inbox-881961/)

- **Bulk attachment downloads:** Available in the Android app specifically.
  - Source: [Android Authority — Gmail vs Inbox](https://www.androidauthority.com/gmail-vs-inbox-881961/)

- **Time-based bundle delivery (scheduled bundles):** Bundles could be set to arrive as a group once per day or week rather than as individual emails. Available on both platforms but particularly valuable on mobile for managing notification noise.
  - Source: [Computerworld — 8 features Gmail can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

---

#### FEATURE MIGRATION TO GMAIL (2018 Redesign & After)

**Features that successfully migrated to Gmail:**

- **Snooze** — moved to Gmail web and mobile in the 2018 redesign. HIGH confidence.
- **Smart Reply** — initially Inbox-only (Nov 2015), expanded to Inbox web (Mar 2016), then to Gmail mobile (2017), then Gmail web (2018). HIGH confidence.
- **Nudges** — AI reminders to follow up on unanswered emails; arrived in Gmail 2018 redesign. HIGH confidence.
- **High-priority notifications** — AI-filtered push alerts; piloted in Inbox Apr 2017, migrated to Gmail app after. HIGH confidence.
- **Hover actions** (archive, delete, snooze, mark-as-read buttons on hover in web list view) — arrived in Gmail 2018 redesign. MEDIUM confidence on Inbox origin.
- **Smart Compose** — launched with Gmail 2018 redesign. However, Smart Compose was a Gmail original feature, NOT an Inbox feature. It is a natural-language autocomplete for composition (vs Smart Reply's one-tap suggested responses, which did originate in Inbox). HIGH confidence this distinction is accurate.
  - Source: [Slate — Don't turn off Gmail's Smart Compose](https://slate.com/technology/2018/10/gmail-smart-compose-accurate-turn-off.html)

**Features that DIED with Inbox / never fully migrated:**

- **Bundles (the full Inbox implementation)** — Gmail's pre-existing tabs (Promotions, Social, Updates) were offered as the alternative, but Inbox Bundles were adaptive, custom-categorized, sweepable grouped views that behaved unlike tabs. Google promised Bundles would come to Gmail; as of December 2019 they had not shipped. They have never shipped as of available records.
  - Source: [Android Police — It's almost 2020 and Gmail still doesn't have Inbox's bundles](https://www.androidpolice.com/2019/12/31/its-almost-2020-and-gmail-still-doesnt-have-inboxs-bundles-which-google-promised-back-in-2018/) (HIGH confidence)
  - Source: [9to5Google — Inbox dies, features that haven't hit Gmail](https://9to5google.com/2019/04/01/inbox-gmail-features-havent-arrived/)

- **Trip Bundles** — Google explicitly admitted this one didn't migrate. Multiple sources note this was the one acknowledged exception. Google Trips app existed briefly as an alternative but was itself shut down in 2019.
  - Source: [Multiple sources including the official shutdown announcement context and MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2018/09/13/google-discontinuing-inbox/)

- **Pin messages** — No equivalent in Gmail as of shutdown (starring and labeling were the suggested workarounds, but they do not replicate pin-to-top behavior).
  - Source: [9to5Google — features that haven't hit Gmail](https://9to5google.com/2019/04/01/inbox-gmail-features-havent-arrived/)

- **Reminders within email** — Inbox allowed creating reminders attached directly to specific emails, with them surfacing at inbox top. This integration did not migrate. Gmail's Tasks integration is separate, not inline in the email list.
  - Source: [Computerworld — 8 features Gmail can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

- **"Save to Inbox" (link saving)** — Did not come to Gmail. Third-party tools filled the gap.
  - Source: [9to5Google — features that haven't hit Gmail](https://9to5google.com/2019/04/01/inbox-gmail-features-havent-arrived/)

- **Natural language search with smart cards** — Inbox supported queries like "confirmation number" returning formatted cards. Gmail search did not replicate this.
  - Source: [9to5Google — features that haven't hit Gmail](https://9to5google.com/2019/04/01/inbox-gmail-features-havent-arrived/)

- **The Done/Sweep model** — Inbox's unified "Done" concept (archive + mark complete) and sweep gestures had no direct equivalent in Gmail's archive model.
  - Source: [Computerworld — 8 features Gmail can't match](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1691918/gmail-vs-inbox.html)

- **Highlights (smart info extraction)** — Inbox extracted real-time data like live flight status, package tracking, and restaurant info and surfaced it inline without opening the email. This did not migrate.
  - Source: [blog.google launch post (primary)](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gmail/an-inbox-that-works-for-you/)

**Google's official framing:** "the new Gmail...incorporates many of the same features you've come to love about Inbox." Matthew Izatt specifically named: snoozing, Smart Reply, Nudges, high-priority notifications. The phrasing "best of Inbox" was used in press coverage paraphrasing the announcement but does not appear verbatim in the official Workspace Updates post (the official post says "we've taken popular Inbox experiences").
  - Source: [Workspace Updates (primary text confirmed)](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2018/09/inbox-by-gmail-shutdown.html)

---

#### RECEPTION

**At launch (Oct 2014):**
- David Pierce, The Verge: "minimalist and lovely, full of layers and easy to navigate. It's remarkably fast and smooth on all platforms, and far better on iOS than the Gmail app." Criticism: low information density, only a few emails visible at once, challenging for high-volume email users. Called it "the future of email" but noted "plenty of algorithm tweaking and design condensing to do."
  - Source: [Wikipedia citing The Verge review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbox_by_Gmail)
- CNET (Sarah Mitroff): criticized that users who already had an organizational system would "find themselves fighting Google's system."
  - Source: [Wikipedia — Inbox by Gmail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbox_by_Gmail)
- Generally framed as an exciting experiment with a devoted but niche user base; never achieved Gmail-scale adoption.

**At shutdown (Sept 2018 – April 2019):**
- Immediate community backlash. Multiple Change.org petitions filed within days, including "Keep Google Inbox alive," "Google, don't kill Inbox!," "Keep Inbox, shut down old Gmail instead!" and several others — from the US, Germany, India, and other countries.
  - Source: [Change.org — multiple petitions](https://www.change.org/p/google-inc-keep-google-inbox)
- Press reaction was broadly critical of Google's decision. PhoneArena ran a piece headlined "Google lies to users about Gmail" challenging Google's claim that "all your favorite Inbox features" were in Gmail.
  - Source: [PhoneArena — Inbox gets its official shutdown date and Google lies to users about Gmail](https://www.phonearena.com/news/Inbox-gets-its-official-shutdown-date-and-Google-lies-to-users-about-Gmail_id114644)
- Gizmodo: "Google Is Killing Inbox — Here Are Some Alternatives"
  - Source: [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/google-is-killing-inbox-here-are-some-alternatives-1829355678)
- 9to5Google (Apr 1, 2019, day before shutdown): catalogued all the features that hadn't arrived in Gmail, implicitly rebuking Google's "migration complete" framing.
  - Source: [9to5Google](https://9to5google.com/2019/04/01/inbox-gmail-features-havent-arrived/)
- Dedicated fanbase: users describing Inbox as having "changed my relationship with email." Retrospective pieces appeared in 2021, still expressing frustration ("I'm still mad"). Shortwave was founded by ex-Googlers explicitly to revive the Inbox experience (launched 2022).
  - Source: [Droid-Life — Google Shutdown Inbox 2 Years Ago and I Still Miss It](https://www.droid-life.com/2021/04/03/google-shutdown-inbox-2-years-ago-and-i-still-miss-it/)
  - Source: [Android Police — Shortwave is Google Inbox's spiritual successor created by ex-Googlers](https://www.androidpolice.com/shortwave-is-google-inboxs-spiritual-successor-created-by-a-team-of-ex-googlers/)

---

### 2. CONFIDENCE LEVELS

| Finding | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Launch date: October 22, 2014 | HIGH | Primary source (blog.google post, Wikipedia, TechCrunch) |
| Public launch date: May 28, 2015 | HIGH | Primary source (gmail.googleblog.com post) |
| Smart Reply launch: November 3, 2015 (mobile) | HIGH | Primary source (blog.google post) |
| Smart Reply web expansion: March 15, 2016 | HIGH | Primary sources (gmail.googleblog.com, 9to5Google) |
| Shutdown announced: September 12, 2018 | HIGH | Primary source (Workspace Updates blog, full text confirmed) |
| Shutdown date: April 2, 2019 | HIGH | MacRumors, Newsweek, multiple outlets consistent |
| Author of launch post: Sundar Pichai | HIGH | WebFetch confirmed byline on blog.google |
| Alex Gawley as product director | HIGH | Business Insider profile with consistent secondary sources |
| Jason Cornwell as lead designer | HIGH | Getty Images caption, Fast Company, AMA records |
| Jacob Bank was NOT an original Inbox team member | HIGH | Timeful acquired May 2015 (7 months post-launch) |
| Bundles never shipped in Gmail | HIGH | Android Police Dec 2019 piece, multiple confirmations |
| Trip Bundles died with Inbox | HIGH | Multiple sources including implied in official messaging |
| Smart Compose originated in Gmail (not Inbox) | HIGH | Multiple sources confirm it debuted in 2018 Gmail redesign |
| Exact "to-do list" philosophy wording | HIGH | Cornwell quote confirmed in multiple interviews |
| Final iOS/Android build numbers | MEDIUM | From Wikipedia, unverified against App Store records |

---

### 3. GAPS

- **Exact invite-wave schedule:** It's documented invites were issued in waves starting October 22, 2014, but the exact pace (how many users had access by December 2014, March 2015, etc.) is not precisely documented in the sources found.
- **Total Inbox user count at shutdown:** Google never disclosed Inbox's peak or final user count. Multiple sources note "it never achieved Gmail-scale adoption" but no figures are available.
- **Exact iOS feature parity vs Android during 2014–2016:** Most platform coverage was Android-focused. The claim that Inbox was "far better on iOS than Gmail for iOS" at launch is cited from The Verge but the specific feature-by-feature iOS/Android parity during early months wasn't specifically documented.
- **The original Google Inbox team size and structure:** The AMA participants (Vijay U, Jason C, Taylor K) used first names only, making full attribution impossible from those records.
- **Whether Highlights (real-time flight/package status) ever landed in Gmail:** Not confirmed either way post-2019.

---

### 4. SURPRISING / CONTRADICTORY FINDINGS

- **Jacob Bank was NOT an Inbox co-creator:** The original question frames him alongside Alex Gawley as a founder of Inbox. In fact, Bank co-founded Timeful, a separate company acquired by Google in May 2015 — seven months after Inbox launched. He joined the Gmail/Inbox team post-acquisition. The "Inbox by Gmail, led by Jacob Bank" framing is not supported by primary sources.

- **Smart Compose is NOT an Inbox-derived feature:** It is often listed in "features that moved from Inbox to Gmail" but this is incorrect. Smart Compose (predictive text completion while composing) originated in the 2018 Gmail redesign. Smart Reply (one-tap response suggestions) was the Inbox-derived feature. The two are frequently conflated.

- **The official shutdown post said "end of March 2019" but the actual shutdown was April 2.** The Workspace Updates blog (September 12, 2018) stated the service would end "at the end of March 2019." Users were later notified ~15 days before actual shutdown, pointing to April 2. MacRumors (March 19, 2019) specifically reported the April 2 date. This is a discrepancy between the original announcement and the actual shutdown date.

- **Google promised Bundles would come to Gmail** when announcing the shutdown, but as of December 2019 (nine months post-shutdown) they had not shipped — and there is no evidence they ever shipped in the Inbox sense.

- **PhoneArena's framing that Google "lied":** While provocative, it was well-supported: Google's official messaging said "you can find your favorite Inbox features in the Gmail app" while Trip Bundles, Pinning, inline Reminders, Save to Inbox, natural language search cards, and the Done/Sweep model were all missing.

---

### 5. SUGGESTED FOLLOW-UPS

1. **Verify Jacob Bank's actual role on Inbox post-Timeful acquisition** — his Crunchbase and PMF Europe interview may clarify whether he led Inbox product management specifically or the broader Gmail group.
2. **Find the exact public-launch blog post text** (May 28, 2015 post "Thanks to you, Inbox by Gmail is now open to everyone") — the body was not retrievable via defuddle; the full Wayback Machine archive may have it.
3. **Check if Bundles ever shipped to Gmail** after December 2019 — the research only confirms absence through end of 2019; the story may have a resolution.
4. **Dig into Inbox for Google Apps (enterprise) timeline** — there are references to a planned enterprise version; unclear if it launched distinctly or just was the same app.
5. **The Inbox Reborn browser extension** (volunteer-maintained, mentioned in Wikipedia) — worth documenting as a notable community response artifact alongside Shortwave.
6. **Verify whether "the best of Inbox is now in Gmail"** appears verbatim in any official Google consumer-facing communication (not just press paraphrase) — the official Workspace Updates post uses different phrasing.

---

---
title: "Inbox by Gmail — Reverse-Engineered UX & Visual Design Specification"
type: research
created: 2026-05-31
subject: Google Inbox (Inbox by Gmail), 2014–2019
status: design reconstruction
---
# Inbox by Gmail — Reverse-Engineered UX & Visual Design Specification

> A reconstruction document intended to let a designer recreate the look, feel, and behavior of Google's deprecated **Inbox by Gmail** (Oct 22, 2014 – Apr 2, 2019). Google never published an official design spec for Inbox, so this document is assembled from primary sources (Google blog posts, developer docs, the official logo SVG), contemporaneous press reviews with screenshots, and faithful community recreations. **Every quantitative value carries a confidence tag** — `[documented]`, `[Material baseline]`, `[recreation]`, or `[estimated]` — so you know what is verbatim vs. inferred.

---

## 0. How to read this document

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[documented]` | Stated in a primary source or extracted directly from the official asset (e.g., the logo SVG). |
| `[Material baseline]` | Not Inbox-specific, but Inbox was built on Material Design 1 (2014) and inherited this value unless it overrode it. |
| `[recreation]` | Taken from a faithful third-party rebuild (chiefly the *Inbox Reborn* extension by ex-Inbox users). Close, but not an official value. |
| `[estimated]` | Best-effort inference from screenshots/branding. Treat as a starting point to eyedropper against the image plates in Appendix B. |

The single most useful action for a recreating designer: open the **image plates in Appendix B** and color-pick directly. The hex values below get you 90% there; the plates settle the last 10%.

---

## 1. Product overview & history

Inbox by Gmail was a **reimagining of email as a to-do list and personal assistant**, built by the Gmail team as a separate product (not a Gmail skin). It was one of the first flagship implementations of **Material Design**, designed *concurrently* with the Material spec itself — some of Inbox's web-density decisions fed back into Material rather than deriving from it.

### Timeline `[documented]`

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **Oct 22, 2014** | Launched, invite-only. Announcement post "An inbox that works for you" authored by **Sundar Pichai**. Simultaneous Web / Android / iOS. |
| Dec 2014 | Reminders + Assists; public AMA by the team. |
| **May 28, 2015** | Opened to everyone (no invite). Shipped **Trip Bundles**, custom signatures, **Undo Send** (10s). |
| Jun 2015 | Trip Bundles detailed; offline trip support. |
| **Nov 3, 2015** | **Smart Reply** launches on Inbox (Android/iOS) — *the first Google product to ship Smart Reply.* |
| Mar 15, 2016 | Smart Reply comes to Inbox **web**. |
| Apr 2016 | **Save to Inbox** (link saving), improved Calendar integration. |
| Apr 2017 | **High-priority notifications** (AI-filtered push). |
| Jun 2018 | Snooze options **"Someday"** and **"Pick Place"** (location snooze) **removed** for low usage. |
| Apr 25, 2018 | Gmail's big redesign absorbs Snooze, Nudges, Smart Reply, high-priority notifications, hover actions. |
| **Sep 12, 2018** | Shutdown **announced** (Workspace Updates blog said "end of March 2019"). |
| **Apr 2, 2019** | Inbox **shut down**. |

### Team `[documented]`
- **Product director:** Alex Gawley (Gmail & Calendar).
- **Lead designer:** Jason Cornwell.
- **Note / myth-bust:** *Jacob Bank* is often credited as an Inbox founder — he is not. He joined Google via the **Timeful acquisition (May 2015)**, seven months after launch, and his time-management tech was folded into Inbox/Calendar afterward.

### Design thesis (verbatim from the launch post) `[documented]`
> "it's not Gmail: it's a completely different type of inbox, designed to focus on what really matters… your inbox becomes a centralized place to keep track of the things you need to get back to… a better way to get back to what matters."

Cornwell's framing: *"kind of like an assistant putting your mail into piles to make it easier to deal with."*

![Inbox main list view, mobile — bundles and cards](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/61/Google_Inbox.png)
*Main Android inbox showing the card list and bundle rows. (© Google, used for reference.)*

---

## 2. Design principles (reconstructed)

1. **Email is a to-do list.** Every item can be *done*, *snoozed*, *pinned*, or *reminded* — verbs of task management, not mail filing.
2. **Information without opening.** Highlights pull the answer (flight time, package status, photo) onto the card face.
3. **Machine does the sorting.** Bundles auto-categorize; the user sweeps, not files.
4. **One primary action, always reachable.** The red FAB anchors creation bottom-right on every surface.
5. **Calm, spacious, white.** Low density by deliberate choice (12–17 rows vs. Gmail's denser list), generous whitespace, a single confident blue.
6. **Motion as feedback.** Swipe reveals, FAB fan-out, the logo's radial fill, the sweep "whoosh," and a sunny empty state reward completion.

---

## 3. Visual design system

### 3.1 Color

**Primary brand / UI blue** — Inbox used Google's proprietary **Google Blue `#4285F4`** as its main UI color (app bar, links, primary accents), *not* Material's palette blue (`#2196F3`). `[documented — two independent sources confirm #4285F4 as the main UI blue]`

**Status-bar / pressed-blue shade** — `#3367D6` (a darker Google Blue, present in the logo SVG; status-bar darkening follows Material convention). `[estimated for status bar; #3367D6 documented in the asset]`

**Logo palette** — extracted directly from the official SVG. Note this multi-blue gradient is the *logo*, broader and more saturated than the single UI blue: `[documented — parsed from official SVG]`

| Role | Hex |
|---|---|
| Envelope flap (medium blue) | `#2A56C6` |
| Envelope shadow (dark blue) | `#1C3AA9` |
| Envelope body (lighter blue) | `#3B78E7` |
| Body mid shade | `#3367D6` |
| Lower-left triangle (cyan-blue) | `#03A9F4` |
| Lower-right triangle (light blue) | `#4FC3F7` |
| Checkmark fill (off-white) | `#E1E1E1` |
| Deep shadow overlay (navy, low opacity) | `#1A237E` |

**Compose FAB red** — the FAB was unambiguously **red** in all coverage. A faithful recreation uses **`#d23f31`**; Google's brand red is `#DB4437`. **No official Inbox FAB hex is documented** — eyedropper Plate F to settle it. `[recreation / estimated]`

**Done / archive green** — the Done action and its checkmark read as green. `#0F9D58` is Google's standard green but is **inferred** for Inbox, not documented. `[estimated]`

**Reminders** — *Correction to common memory:* there is **no documented yellow reminder card background.** The reminder **icon was blue** (the asset was named `ic_reminder_blue_24dp`), and the reminder-creation mini-FAB used `#4285F4`. The "yellow reminders" association most likely conflates the **pin's yellow variant** or Google Keep's yellow. Treat any yellow reminder styling as **unverified** until you color-pick Plate H. `[documented: blue icon; yellow background: refuted/unverified]`

**Neutrals & dividers** `[recreation]`

| Role | Hex |
|---|---|
| Card / row background | `#FFFFFF` |
| Page background (behind cards) | `#F2F2F2` |
| Row divider | `#DDDDDD` |
| Primary text | ~`#212121` |
| Secondary text (snippet, time) | `#5F6368` / `#616161` |

**Bundle category accent colors** — Inbox distinguished bundles primarily by **bespoke icon art**, not text color. The per-category colors below come from the *Inbox Reborn* recreation and are the designer's interpretation, **not verified originals** — use as a plausible starting palette only. `[recreation, low confidence]`

| Bundle | Recreation color |
|---|---|
| Updates | orange `rgb(255,104,57)` |
| Promos | cyan `rgb(0,188,212)` |
| Forums | indigo `rgb(63,81,181)` |
| Social | red `rgb(219,68,55)` |
| Travel / Trips | purple `rgb(156,39,176)` |
| Finance | green `rgb(103,159,56)` |
| Purchases | brown `rgb(121,85,72)` |

### 3.2 Typography

**Typeface: Roboto** for the entire UI. `[documented]` Inbox **predated Google Sans / Product Sans** (those arrived with Google's Sept 2015 logo change), so the "Inbox" wordmark in the app bar was set in Roboto (white, ~20sp, Regular/Light).

Material Design 1 type scale, mapped to Inbox elements: `[Material baseline; mapping estimated]`

| Element | Size | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| App-bar wordmark "Inbox" | ~20sp | Roboto Regular/Light, white |
| Sender name (read) | 16sp | Roboto Regular |
| Sender name (unread) | 16sp | Roboto **Medium (500)** |
| Subject line | 16sp / 14sp | Roboto Regular |
| Snippet (secondary) | 14sp | Roboto Regular, `#5F6368` |
| Timestamp (right-aligned) | 12sp | Roboto Regular (Caption) |
| Bundle header | ~16sp | Roboto Medium |
| Buttons | 14sp | Roboto Medium, ALL CAPS |

Full MD1 scale for reference: Title 20sp Medium · Subheading 16/15sp · Body2 14sp Medium · Body1 14sp · Caption 12sp · Headline 24sp · Display1 34sp.

### 3.3 Iconography
- **Style:** Material line icons (outlined, thin stroke, **24dp** baseline). `[Material baseline]`
- **Bundle icons:** Travel = airplane · Purchases = shopping bag/tag · Finance = dollar · Social = people · Updates = bell · Forums = chat bubble · Promos = tag. `[documented]`
- **Action icons:** Done = circular **checkmark** · Pin = custom **thumbtack** (not in the stock Material set at launch — Google had to add it later) · Snooze = **clock** · Reminder = blue pointing-finger · Compose = **pencil**. `[documented]`
- **App icon:** opened envelope with a checkmark emerging; multi-blue composition; animates a **radial color fill** as the envelope opens and the check rises on launch. `[documented]`

![Inbox app icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Google_Inbox_by_Gmail_logo.png)
*Official app icon (Wikimedia Commons, public domain).*

### 3.4 Layout, grid, density `[Material baseline unless noted]`
- **8dp baseline grid** throughout; touch targets ≥ **48×48dp**.
- **Screen margins:** 16dp mobile, 24dp desktop/tablet. Content keyline at **72dp** from the left (after avatar/icon).
- **App bar height:** 56dp portrait mobile, 64dp desktop. Status bar 24dp.
- **List rows:** MD three-line tile = 88dp standard / 76dp dense. **Inbox overrode these** to hit a deliberately spacious 12–17 rows on web; exact custom heights were never published. `[documented that it was customized; values not documented]`
- **Cards:** each message/bundle is a Material **card** at 2dp resting elevation.

### 3.5 Elevation & shadow `[Material baseline]`

| Component | Resting | Raised |
|---|---|---|
| FAB | 6dp | 12dp (pressed) |
| Card | 2dp | 8dp (picked up) |
| App bar | 4dp | — |
| Nav drawer | 16dp | — |
| Dialog | 24dp | — |

CSS shadow recipes:
- 2dp card: `0 2px 2px 0 rgba(0,0,0,.14), 0 3px 1px -2px rgba(0,0,0,.2), 0 1px 5px 0 rgba(0,0,0,.12)`
- 6dp FAB: `0 6px 10px 0 rgba(0,0,0,.14), 0 1px 18px 0 rgba(0,0,0,.12), 0 3px 5px -1px rgba(0,0,0,.2)`

### 3.6 Motion principles
- **Material easing & duration:** standard MD1 curves (`fast-out-slow-in`), ~200–300ms transitions. `[Material baseline]`
- **Signature motions:** logo radial fill on launch; FAB plus→pencil rotate-and-cut swap; FAB speed-dial fan-out; swipe-card slide revealing the action color beneath; pin "shoot out and back" toggle; bundle expand/collapse; the sweep "whoosh"; sunny empty state. `[documented]`

## 4. Core components & behaviors

### 4.1 App bar & navigation
- Top app bar in **blue `#4285F4`** with white "Inbox" wordmark and a **hamburger** opening a left nav drawer (16dp elevation). `[documented]`
- Drawer sections: **Inbox**, the bundles (Travel, Purchases, Finance, Social, Updates, Forums, Promos, Low Priority), **Trips**, **Snoozed**, **Done**, **Reminders**, plus settings. `[documented]`
- A **"Pinned only" toggle switch** sat in the app bar — flipping it filtered the list to pinned items only. `[documented]`

![Nav drawer / sidebar with bundle list](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/02-Inbox-Inbox-And-Slide.png)
*Inbox list + slide-out navigation. (© MakeUseOf, reference use.)*

### 4.2 The email card / list item
A white card per message: sender (Medium if unread), subject, secondary snippet in gray, right-aligned timestamp, optional avatar/logo, and — crucially — **Highlights** rendered on the face (thumbnails, chips). Cards group under **time separators** ("Today", "Yesterday") and under **bundle headers**.

### 4.3 Bundles (auto-categorization) `[documented]`
The flagship organizing feature — "the next generation of Gmail's labels." Related mail auto-groups into a **single collapsible row** with a category header, icon, and message count; expand to see members.

- **Default set (9):** Travel, Purchases, Finance, Social, Updates, Forums, Promos, **Low Priority**, plus user **Custom bundles** (built on Gmail labels).
- **Per-bundle delivery schedule:** *Show in inbox* (real-time) · *Once a day* (7 AM) · *Once a week* (Mon 7 AM) — great for taming Promos.
- **Custom bundles:** create a Gmail label → enable "bundle messages in inbox" → optionally set frequency.
- **Sweep:** a checkmark on the bundle header marks **all unpinned** members **Done** in one tap (they go to the **Done** archive, not deleted).
- **Quirk:** some bundled mail could be auto-marked Done and **never surface in the main inbox** — a known source of "where did my email go?" friction.
- The category taxonomy outlived Inbox: Gmail search still honors `category:travel`, `category:purchases`, `category:finance`, `category:reservations`.

![Purchases bundle expanded](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/04-Inbox-Purchases-Label.png)
*An expanded bundle with category header. (© MakeUseOf, reference use.)*

### 4.4 Highlights `[documented]`
Key info extracted to the card face so you needn't open the mail. Rendered as compact **chips / mini-cards** above or alongside the message, often with imagery and a one-tap **Action**.

**Ten documented highlight types:** Flight · Bus · Car rental · Train reservations (each with departure/arrival + a destination image; flights add **live status** + *Check In*); **Order** (price, est. delivery, product image); **Parcel delivery** (live tracking badge + *Track Package*); **Hotel** (+ property image); **Restaurant** (+ image); **Ticketed event** (venue/date + *View Tickets*); **Invoice**.

**Data sources:** schema.org structured markup embedded by senders (FlightReservation, ParcelDelivery, OrderStatus, etc., requiring Google whitelist approval) **and** NLP content analysis for known senders. The *same* markup simultaneously powered Inbox Highlights, Gmail Actions, Google Now cards, and Calendar event creation.

![Highlights and Assists on cards](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiAdmZgT10aBgfBVQza_2vTcLkEEvwEZt9qEIKeUF6LRTaoseUr6gnWArkfg29VUm5EwloB5g2t3dRrhFTerOwgctquGu8aAOyUCdmPwmnSTE-MOofvyLKzgtG5OHVSqj2heeKpVw/s1600/inbox5.png)
*Highlights / Assists surfaced inline. (© Google / Google System blog, reference use.)*

### 4.5 Trip bundles `[documented]`
Auto-assembled travel itineraries (launched May/Jun 2015). Inbox scanned confirmation emails and grouped flights, hotels, car rentals, restaurant and event reservations by date/destination into one card bearing a **destination photo**.

- **Collapsed:** destination + dates card; trips also listed in the left nav under **Trips** (upcoming + past).
- **Expanded:** an agenda prioritizing **times, dates, confirmation numbers** — flight (terminal/gate/duration), hotel (check-in/out), car rental, dinner — with source emails listed below. Canonical Google demo: Austin → London (Heathrow), Hertz rental, week at "The Blue Hotel."
- **Dynamic:** delays/gate changes update automatically. **Offline-saveable.** **Shareable** via email (Dec 2015). Third-party (HotelTonight, Eat24) integrated.

![Trip bundle itinerary](https://www.droid-life.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/06/inbox-trip-bundles1.jpg)
*Expanded trip bundle. (© Droid-Life, reference use.)*

### 4.6 Reminders & Assists `[documented]`
- **Reminders** are first-class inbox items (not emails) — created via the FAB, and pinnable/snoozable/done-able like any item. They sit inline among messages.
- **Assists:** Google auto-enriches a reminder — a "call [business]" reminder gains the phone number and hours; travel/package reminders gain itinerary/tracking detail.
- Later: follow-up reminders for sent mail awaiting a reply.
- *(Styling: the reminder icon was blue; a distinct yellow card background is not documented — see §3.1.)*

![Reminders](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/09-Inbox-Reminders.png)
*Reminders with suggestions. (© MakeUseOf, reference use.)*

### 4.7 The FAB / Speed Dial / Compose `[documented]`
- Circular **red** FAB, bottom-right, 56dp (mini sub-FABs 40dp), 6dp elevation; plus icon at rest.
- Tapping expands a **speed dial** (Google's internal name) fanning **upward**: **Compose** (pencil), **Reminder** (blue finger), and **frequent-contact avatar chips** for one-tap compose-to-person.
- **Icon transition:** plus rotates and cuts out as the pencil rotates and cuts in (a fast swap, not a morph).
- Compose opens as a sheet (bottom sheet on mobile). Replies are inline at the thread bottom in a light Material card.

![Compose FAB fan-out with contacts](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/10-Inbox-Compose-Windows.png)
*FAB expanded with frequent contacts. (© MakeUseOf, reference use.)*

### 4.8 Done / Sweep / Pin `[documented]`
- **Done** = archive-equivalent; a green **checkmark** sends mail to the **Done** label (recover by opening it and tapping the check again).
- **Sweep** = mark all unpinned items in a section/bundle Done in one action (icon: checkmark with speed lines). Reviewers described the feel as a satisfying "whoosh."
- **Pin** = Inbox's star; **blue pin** icon; pinned items survive a sweep and can be isolated via the "Pinned only" toggle or `is:pinned`. Pin toggle animation: the pin shoots out in its facing direction, then back in reversed as the button restyles.

![Pinned items](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/08-Inbox-Pinned.png)
*Pinned messages. (© MakeUseOf, reference use.)*

### 4.9 Swipe gestures `[documented]`
- **Swipe right = Done** (green reveal + checkmark beneath the sliding card).
- **Swipe left = Snooze** (reveals the snooze picker; clock-style icon beneath).
- **Fixed, not user-configurable** (unlike later Gmail). Material swipe-to-dismiss physics.

![Swipe shortcuts](https://static0.makeuseofimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/07-Inbox-Sliding-Shortcuts.png)
*Right = Done, left = Snooze. (© MakeUseOf, reference use.)*

### 4.10 Snooze `[documented]`
Preset options (full set before the Jun 2018 trim):
- **Later today**
- **Tomorrow**
- **This weekend** / **Later this week**
- **Next week**
- **Someday** *(random future time — removed Jun 2018)*
- **Pick date & time** (custom picker)
- **Snooze until you arrive at a place** / "Pick Place" — geofenced to Work/Home *(removed Jun 2018)*

Mar 2015 added user-set **morning/afternoon/evening** default times (linked to Keep), prompting e.g. "Change your morning time to 7:30 AM?" Jul 2015 added **suggested** snooze times with a clock-icon animation. Snoozed items return to the **top** of the inbox at the chosen time/place; a clock icon marks them; a **Snoozed** view lists all pending.

![Snooze options](https://www.droid-life.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Inbox-Snooze1.jpg)
*Snooze preset menu. (© Droid-Life, reference use.)*

### 4.11 Smart Reply `[documented]`
- Debuted on Inbox **Nov 3, 2015** (mobile), **first Google product** to ship it; web Mar 2016.
- Showed **three** short suggested replies at the bottom of an eligible message; tap to load into the compose field (edit or send-as-is — "two-tap email"). Adaptive: unused suggestion styles fade for that contact.
- Tech: two coupled **LSTM** networks (encoder→thought vector→decoder), English only at launch. Grew to ~**12%** of Inbox mobile replies. (Early bug: it over-suggested "I love you" until probabilities were normalized.)

![Smart Reply suggestions](https://static0.anpoimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/nexus2cee_Screenshot-from-2016-03-15-15-33-14.png)
*Three Smart Reply chips (web). (© Android Police, reference use.)*

### 4.12 Undo `[documented]`
A **dark/black snackbar** with an **UNDO** text button appears at the bottom immediately after Done/Sweep/Snooze/Delete. Exact timeout undocumented (~Material 2–5s). Separately, **Undo Send** offered a 10s send-cancel window (added Jun 2015).

### 4.13 Search `[documented, lightly]`
Top search field with **contact suggestions** as you type and **natural-language smart results** — e.g. typing "confirmation number" returned formatted booking cards from Highlight data. This structured search notably **did not** survive into Gmail.

### 4.14 Save to Inbox `[documented]`
From Apr 2016: save web links into Inbox as items (desktop Chrome extension; mobile OS share sheet). Saved URLs grouped in a **Saved** bundle, snoozable like anything else. Removed from Android Aug 2018.

### 4.15 Empty state `[documented, with correction]`
At inbox zero Inbox showed a **sunny-sky illustration** as a reward. *Correction:* the specific copy **"Woohoo!"** is **not confirmed** in sources, and the well-known "woman reading in a garden/sun" flat illustration belongs to **Gmail's** empty state — do not assume it was Inbox's exact art. Recreate "a calm, sunny illustration on clearing the inbox" and verify against a live capture (Appendix C).

## 5. Platform differences `[documented]`

| Aspect | Web (inbox.google.com) | Android | iOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design intent | Same language, denser list (12–17 rows) | **Mobile-first**; swipe-centric | Mobile-first; praised as *better than Gmail's own iOS app* at launch (The Verge) |
| Smart Reply | Added Mar 2016 | Launch Nov 2015 | Launch Nov 2015 |
| Save to Inbox | Chrome extension | Share sheet (removed Aug 2018) | Share sheet |
| Canned responses | Desktop-only | — | — |
| Bulk attachment download | — | Android-specific | — |
| Snooze-by-location | n/a (no device GPS) | Yes | Yes |

Core swipe (right=Done / left=Snooze) and sweep were mobile-optimized; web exposed equivalents via hover buttons + keyboard shortcuts.

## 6. What migrated to Gmail vs. what died `[documented]`

**Survived (into the Apr 2018 Gmail redesign and after):** Snooze · Smart Reply · Nudges (follow-up reminders) · High-priority notifications · Hover actions.
**Died with Inbox / never shipped to Gmail:** Bundles (the adaptive, sweepable kind — *promised but never delivered*) · **Trip Bundles** (explicitly acknowledged as not migrating; standalone Google Trips also shut down 2019) · **Pin** · inline **Reminders/Assists** · **Save to Inbox** · natural-language **smart search cards** · the unified **Done/Sweep** model · **Highlights** (live flight/package extraction).

**Myth-bust:** **Smart Compose is NOT an Inbox feature** — it originated in the 2018 Gmail redesign. The Inbox-born ML feature was **Smart Reply**. The two are frequently conflated.

Reception: a devoted-but-niche following; the shutdown drew Change.org petitions and accusations that Google overstated the migration. **Shortwave** (2022, by ex-Googlers) was built explicitly to revive the Inbox experience.

The design document is written to your vault. A background fact-checking pass is still running on the highest-risk claims (dates, hex values, the reminder-color and "Woohoo!" questions) — I'll patch the doc if it turns up anything, and you'll see me follow up.

## What I built

**`/Users/alexhedtke/Exobrain/Research/Google Inbox UX Design Document.md`** — a hand-it-to-a-designer reconstruction spec, ~3,500 words, built from five parallel research threads (visual system, bundles/highlights, interactions, history/platforms, and an image hunt) and cross-checked against primary sources.

It's structured as:

- **History & team** — full timeline (Oct 22 2014 invite-only → May 28 2015 public → Sep 12 2018 announced → Apr 2 2019 dead), with the verbatim design thesis.
- **Visual design system** — color (the `#4285F4` UI blue, the full logo palette extracted from the official SVG, the red FAB, neutrals, bundle colors), Roboto type scale, Material line iconography, the 8dp grid/density, and elevation/shadow recipes.
- **Component-by-component behavior** — app bar/nav, the email card, Bundles, Highlights (all 10 types), Trip bundles, Reminders + Assists, the FAB speed-dial fan-out, Done/Sweep/Pin, swipe gestures, the full Snooze preset list, Smart Reply, undo, search, Save to Inbox, and the empty state.
- **Platform matrix**, **migration table** (what lived on in Gmail vs. what died), a **confidence summary**, copy-paste **CSS design tokens**, and **14 image plates** with ~50 verified-live screenshot URLs.

## A few things worth flagging (I corrected common myths in the doc)

I made a point of tagging every number as `[documented]`, `[Material baseline]`, `[recreation]`, or `[estimated]`, because **Google never published an Inbox design spec.** Notable corrections the research surfaced:

- **The "yellow reminders" memory appears to be wrong** — the reminder *icon* was blue (`ic_reminder_blue`); no source documents a yellow reminder card background. Likely a conflation with the pin's yellow variant or Google Keep.
- **"Woohoo!" empty-state copy is unconfirmed** — there was a sunny illustration, but the famous "woman reading in a garden" art is actually *Gmail's*, not Inbox's.
- **Smart Compose was a Gmail original**, not an Inbox feature (Smart *Reply* is the Inbox-born one).
- **Jacob Bank wasn't an Inbox founder** — he arrived via the Timeful acquisition seven months after launch. Lead designer was Jason Cornwell; product director Alex Gawley.

**Honest limitation:** exact hexes for the FAB red, Done green, and the custom dense row-heights were never officially published. The single best way to nail them is to color-pick the image plates (Appendix B) or decompile the final Inbox APK (Android 1.78) — I noted both paths in Appendix C.

One licensing note: all the screenshot URLs are copyrighted press captures (fine for an internal design reference, not commercial redistribution); only the two Wikimedia logo files are public domain.

The verification pass came back clean — all 13 claims held up. One refinement is warranted: the verifier was more cautious than my draft on the `#4285F4` app-bar blue, classifying it as *plausible/inferred* rather than firmly documented (no official Google spec pins the app bar to that exact value; it's the canonical Google Blue and widely accepted, but inferred). Let me soften that tag for accuracy.

blocks.text:
Got it — I've captured the other two answers: **full client with compose/reply/send**, and the backlink should **open the email back in the Inbox clone (launching the app if it isn't running) and fall back to Gmail web only if the clone can't serve it.** Both are very doable, and the auth choice actually matters a lot for how cleanly the "Done = archive" and bundle/label behavior maps — so let's walk through Option 2 properly.

## Gmail API (OAuth) — the hypothetical walkthrough

### What you'd set up once (~15–20 min, all in Google Cloud Console)

1. **Create a Google Cloud project** at console.cloud.google.com (e.g. "Inbox Clone"). Free.
2. **Enable the Gmail API** for that project (APIs & Services → Library → Gmail API → Enable).
3. **Configure the OAuth consent screen** → User type **External** (required for a personal @gmail.com; "Internal" is Workspace-only). Fill in app name, your email for support + developer fields.
4. **Add scopes** — for a full client with triage *and* compose you'd request:
   - `gmail.modify` — read messages, change labels, archive, mark read/unread. **Archiving = removing the `INBOX` label, which is exactly how Inbox's "Done" worked.** This is the key reason the API is a better fit than IMAP.
   - `gmail.send` — send/reply.
   - (Optional `gmail.labels` for managing custom labels — used for Snooze/Bundles.)
   - Deliberately **not** `https://mail.google.com/` (full access incl. permanent delete) — we don't need destructive power.
5. **Create credentials** → OAuth client ID → application type **Desktop app** → download `client_secret.json`.
6. **First run of the app:** it opens your browser, you sign in and approve. Because the app is "unverified," you'll see a warning screen — click **Advanced → Go to Inbox Clone (unsafe)**. That's expected for a personal app you wrote yourself. It then stores a **refresh token** locally (`token.json`, gitignored). Every run after that is silent — no re-login.

### The one gotcha worth knowing
If you leave the consent screen in **"Testing"** publishing status, Google **expires the refresh token after 7 days** — you'd have to re-auth weekly. The fix: set publishing status to **"In production"** (you do *not* need to submit for Google verification for personal use — you just keep clicking past the unverified warning the first time). Then the token persists indefinitely. I'd configure it this way so you set it up once and forget it.

### Why it's the better foundation for an Inbox clone

| | Gmail API (OAuth) | IMAP + app password |
|---|---|---|
| "Done" / archive | Native — remove `INBOX` label. Perfect Inbox semantics. | Works (move/expunge) but clunkier, folder-based. |
| Threads | First-class `threadId` grouping | You reconstruct threading yourself from headers |
| Labels / Bundles / Snooze | Native labels — ideal for custom Bundle + Snooze labels | Maps to IMAP folders, messier |
| Incremental sync | `history.list` (fast, push-capable) | Re-poll folders |
| Send | `gmail.send` (proper threading/References) | SMTP (you build MIME + threading) |
| Setup cost | ~15 min GCP setup + unverified warning | ~3 min (just generate an app password) |
| Long-term robustness | High | Google keeps tightening IMAP; fine for now |

**My recommendation:** go with the **Gmail API**. The setup tax is one-time and modest, and since you want a *full client with compose* plus faithful Inbox "Done/archive/label" behavior, the label-native model pays for itself immediately. IMAP would have me hand-rolling threading and faking archive semantics that the API gives natively.

### How the backlink requirement gets built (either way)
Independent of the auth choice, I'll implement the backlink as a **custom URL scheme** (e.g. `inboxclone://thread/<id>`) registered by a tiny launcher `.app` in `~/Desktop/Apps/`. When Things 3 fires it: the launcher checks whether the local server is running → starts it if not → opens that exact thread in the clone. If the message can't be served (e.g., the clone is broken/unreachable), it falls back to the Gmail web permalink. So the Things task gets one link that "just works," with Gmail as the safety net — exactly what you described.

---

Now that you've seen what Option 2 entails — **want me to proceed with the Gmail API (my recommendation), or would you rather keep it lightweight with IMAP + app password?** Once you pick, I'll scaffold the project (gitignored creds + README per the repo's privacy rules), then build the backend connection and the Inbox-faithful frontend from the design spec we just wrote.

#!/bin/bash
# YouTube Downloader app launcher
# - If server already running, just open the browser
# - Otherwise start it, then open the browser, and keep the dock icon alive
#   for the lifetime of the server. Cmd+Q (quit) kills the server.

set -e
PORT=5005
URL="http://127.0.0.1:$PORT"

# Make sure Homebrew + uv are findable when launched from Finder
export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"

if lsof -i tcp:$PORT -sTCP:LISTEN >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    open "$URL"
    exit 0
fi

# Resources is where Info.plist points us to find app.py
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../Resources" && pwd)"
cd "$SCRIPT_DIR"

# Open the browser shortly after the server starts
( for _ in {1..40}; do
    if curl -sf "$URL" -o /dev/null 2>&1; then open "$URL"; exit; fi
    sleep 0.25
  done ) &

# Replace this process with uv so the dock icon represents the running server.
# When user quits the app, uv (and Flask) get the signal and exit.
exec uv run --script app.py

# Inbox — a Google Inbox clone over the Gmail API

A local, single-user email client that recreates the look and triage model of the
deprecated **Inbox by Gmail**, with one-tap **Send to Things 3** that backlinks
straight to the email.

Built from the design spec at `Exobrain/Research/Google Inbox UX Design Document.md`.

## Architecture
- **Backend:** `app.py` — Flask + Gmail API (`uv run --script`, deps inline via PEP 723).
- **Frontend:** `templates/index.html` + `static/{style.css,app.js}` — vanilla SPA styled to the Inbox spec.
- **Launcher:** `~/Desktop/Apps/Inbox.app` — starts the server, opens the browser, and handles `inboxclone://` deep links.
- **Port:** `http://127.0.0.1:5008`

## Triage model (maps Inbox semantics onto native Gmail labels)
| Inbox action | Gmail mechanism |
|---|---|
| Done | remove `INBOX` label (archive) |
| Pin | `STARRED` label |
| Snooze | remove `INBOX` + add `Snoozed`; background scheduler re-adds `INBOX` at wake time (state in `snooze.db`) |
| Bundles | native categories (Promos/Social/Updates/Forums) + keyword classifier for Travel/Purchases/Finance |

## Send to Things 3
Each thread/card has a **Send to Things** action. It fires:
```
things:///add?title=<subject>&notes=<backlink + gmail fallback + sender/snippet>
```
The note's backlink is `inboxclone://thread/<threadId>?gmail=<gmail permalink>`.
Tapping it in Things launches **Inbox.app** (starting the server if needed) and reopens
the exact thread; if the clone can't serve it, it falls back to the Gmail web permalink.

## Credentials (GITIGNORED — must be rebuilt on a fresh clone)
This repo intentionally ships **no credentials**. To run:
1. Google Cloud Console → create a project → enable the **Gmail API**.
2. OAuth consent screen → **External**, add yourself as the user; set publishing status
   to **In production** (avoids the 7-day refresh-token expiry that "Testing" imposes).
3. Create an **OAuth client ID → Desktop app**; download the JSON.
4. Save it as `credentials/client_secret.json`.
5. First launch opens a Google consent page — approve (click *Advanced → Go to app* past
   the unverified-app warning). A `credentials/token.json` is written (chmod 600) and reused.

Scopes used: `gmail.modify` (read/label/archive) + `gmail.send` (compose/reply). No delete scope.

## Run
- Double-click `~/Desktop/Apps/Inbox.app`, or:
- `cd ~/Documents/inbox-clone && uv run --script app.py`

input.content:
-- Inbox.app launcher + inboxclone:// deep-link handler
property projDir : (POSIX path of (path to home folder)) & "Documents/inbox-clone"
property serverURL : "http://127.0.0.1:5008"
property envPath : "/opt/homebrew/bin:" & (POSIX path of (path to home folder)) & ".local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"

on serverUp()
	try
		do shell script "curl -sf " & serverURL & "/api/health -o /dev/null"
		return true
	on error
		return false
	end try
end serverUp

on ensureServer()
	if serverUp() then return true
	do shell script "cd " & quoted form of projDir & " && export PATH=" & envPath & " && nohup uv run --script app.py > server.log 2>&1 &"
	repeat 90 times
		delay 0.5
		if serverUp() then return true
	end repeat
	return false
end ensureServer

on run
	ensureServer()
	open location serverURL
end run

on open location this_URL
	set ok to ensureServer()
	set threadId to ""
	set gmailURL to ""
	try
		set afterScheme to text ((offset of "thread/" in this_URL) + 7) thru -1 of this_URL
		if afterScheme contains "?" then
			set threadId to text 1 thru ((offset of "?" in afterScheme) - 1) of afterScheme
		else
			set threadId to afterScheme
		end if
	end try
	try
		if this_URL contains "gmail=" then
			set rawGmail to text ((offset of "gmail=" in this_URL) + 6) thru -1 of this_URL
			set gmailURL to do shell script "python3 -c 'import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.unquote(sys.argv[1]))' " & quoted form of rawGmail
		end if
	end try
	if ok and threadId is not "" then
		open location serverURL & "/thread/" & threadId
	else if gmailURL is not "" then
		open location gmailURL
	else
		open location serverURL
	end if
end open location

---
name: project_inbox_clone_app
description: Inbox clone email app (Gmail API) with Send-to-Things backlinks; Flask :5008, launcher + inboxclone:// scheme
metadata:
  type: project

**Inbox** — a Google Inbox clone built 2026-05-31. Local Flask app over the **Gmail API** that recreates Inbox-by-Gmail's look + triage model, with one-tap **Send to Things 3** that backlinks to the exact email.

- **Code (source of truth):** `~/Documents/inbox-clone/` — `app.py` (uv inline-script Flask + Gmail API), `templates/index.html`, `static/{style.css,app.js}`. Styled from [[project_exobrain]]'s research doc `Exobrain/Research/Google Inbox UX Design Document.md`.

Set OAuth consent to **In production** to avoid the 7-day refresh-token expiry of "Testing" status. First-run consent URL gets buffered in `server.log` unless `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`.

- **Send-to-Things:** builds `things:///add` with notes = `inboxclone://thread/<id>?gmail=<permalink>` + Gmail fallback + sender/snippet. Verified end-to-end 2026-05-31.
- **Not yet built:** Snoozed/Done list views (nav stubs), Highlights chips, search backend, custom snooze date/time + snooze-by-location, compose verified-send (compose UI + reply wired, send path tested via API).

## Done — your Inbox clone is live

It's open in your browser now, signed in as **alex.hedtke@gmail.com**, showing your real mail bucketed into bundles (right now: Purchases 4, Promos 5, Updates 13).

### What got built
- **`~/Documents/inbox-clone/`** — Flask backend over the **Gmail API** + a vanilla SPA styled straight from the design spec we wrote (the `#4285F4` app bar, Roboto, white cards on `#F2F2F2`, the red speed-dial FAB, hover + swipe actions, snooze menu, sunny empty state).
- **`~/Desktop/Apps/Inbox.app`** — launcher that starts the server and handles the `inboxclone://` deep links. Double-click it anytime; if the server's already up it just opens the window.

### Verified working end-to-end
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Gmail OAuth (gmail.modify + gmail.send) | ✅ authed as you |
| Inbox load + bundle bucketing | ✅ (keyword classifier even caught "1-800 Contacts order" → Purchases) |
| Thread fetch (HTML+text, reply Message-ID) | ✅ |
| `inboxclone://` deep link → opens the exact thread | ✅ fired |
| **Send to Things 3** with backlink | ✅ task created in Things with `inboxclone://thread/...` + Gmail fallback in notes (test task cleaned up) |

### The triage model (faithful to Inbox)
**Done** = archive (remove `INBOX`) · **Pin** = star · **Snooze** = real, with a background scheduler that re-files the mail to your inbox at wake time · **Bundles** = native Gmail categories + Travel/Purchases/Finance heuristics. Swipe right = Done, left = Snooze; hover a card for the action buttons; the **✓-list icon** on any card or in the reader is Send-to-Things.

### The backlink behavior you asked for
A Things task's link is `inboxclone://thread/<id>` → launches Inbox.app (starting the server if it's closed) and reopens that exact email; **falls back to the Gmail web permalink** only if the clone can't serve it.

### Two things worth knowing
1. **The 7-day token gotcha:** make sure your OAuth consent screen is set to **"In production"** (not "Testing") in Google Cloud Console — otherwise Google expires the refresh token weekly and you'd have to re-auth. If it's already in production, you're set for good.
2. **Not yet built (clearly stubbed):** the Snoozed/Done *list* views (the nav items are there but return empty for now), Highlights chips on cards, a real search backend, and the custom snooze date/time + snooze-by-location pickers. FINANCE_RE = re.compile(r"\b(statement|payment|invoice|balance|transaction|deposit|bank|credit card|autopay|bill is)\b", re.I)

# Highlight chips — lightweight heuristic stand-in for Inbox's schema.org/ML highlights
PRICE_RE = re.compile(r"\$\s?\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d{2})?")
TRACK_RE = re.compile(r"\b(out for delivery|arriving today|arriving|delivered|has shipped|shipped|on its way|tracking)\b", re.I)
FLIGHT_HL_RE = re.compile(r"\b(flight|boarding|departs?|gate|check[- ]?in)\b", re.I)
ORDER_RE = re.compile(r"\border\s*#?\s*[\w-]{3,}", re.I)


def compute_highlights(subject, snippet, bundle):
    blob = f"{subject} {snippet}"
    chips = []
    if bundle == "Travel" or FLIGHT_HL_RE.search(blob):
        chips.append({"icon": "flight", "text": "Travel"})
    tm = TRACK_RE.search(blob)
    if tm:
        chips.append({"icon": "local_shipping", "text": tm.group(0).title()})
    om = ORDER_RE.search(blob)
    if om:
        chips.append({"icon": "receipt_long", "text": om.group(0).strip()[:22]})
    pm = PRICE_RE.search(blob)
    if pm:
        chips.append({"icon": "payments", "text": pm.group(0).replace(" ", "")})
    seen, out = set(), []
    for c in chips:
        if c["icon"] in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(c["icon"])
        out.append(c)
    return out[:2]


app = Flask(__name__)

text: When I try to open the app it says "Stack overflow -2706"

blocks.text:
That's an AppleScript recursion bug — error **-2706 is `errAEStackOverflow`**. The cause: my launcher defines an `on open location` handler, but inside it (and in `on run`) it calls `open location …` to open the browser. AppleScript routes that call *back into the same handler* instead of to the system, so it recurses until the stack blows.

The fix is to open URLs via the shell (`do shell script "open …"`) instead of the `open location` command, so it can't re-enter the handler. Let me rewrite and rebuild the launcher.

blocks.name: Write

input.content:
-- Inbox.app launcher + inboxclone:// deep-link handler
-- NOTE: never call `open location` here — this script defines `on open location`,
-- and calling the command re-enters the handler (errAEStackOverflow -2706).
-- Always open URLs via the shell `open` command instead.
property projDir : (POSIX path of (path to home folder)) & "Documents/inbox-clone"
property serverURL : "http://127.0.0.1:5008"
property envPath : "/opt/homebrew/bin:" & (POSIX path of (path to home folder)) & ".local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"

on serverUp()
	try
		do shell script "curl -sf " & serverURL & "/api/health -o /dev/null"
		return true
	on error
		return false
	end try
end serverUp

on ensureServer()
	if serverUp() then return true
	do shell script "cd " & quoted form of projDir & " && export PATH=" & envPath & " && nohup uv run --script app.py > server.log 2>&1 &"
	repeat 90 times
		delay 0.5
		if serverUp() then return true
	end repeat
	return false
end ensureServer

on openURL(u)
	do shell script "open " & quoted form of u
end openURL

on run
	ensureServer()
	openURL(serverURL)
end run

on open location this_URL
	set ok to ensureServer()
	set threadId to ""
	set gmailURL to ""
	try
		set afterScheme to text ((offset of "thread/" in this_URL) + 7) thru -1 of this_URL
		if afterScheme contains "?" then
			set threadId to text 1 thru ((offset of "?" in afterScheme) - 1) of afterScheme
		else
			set threadId to afterScheme
		end if
	end try
	try
		if this_URL contains "gmail=" then
			set rawGmail to text ((offset of "gmail=" in this_URL) + 6) thru -1 of this_URL
			set gmailURL to do shell script "python3 -c 'import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.unquote(sys.argv[1]))' " & quoted form of rawGmail
		end if
	end try
	if ok and threadId is not "" then
		openURL(serverURL & "/thread/" & threadId)
	else if gmailURL is not "" then
		openURL(gmailURL)
	else
		openURL(serverURL)
	end if
end open location

Quick note on the approach and why: true Gmail *push* (Pub/Sub `users().watch()`) requires Google to POST to a **public HTTPS endpoint** — impossible for a `127.0.0.1` app without running a tunnel. Live sync is in and verified. A fresh tab is open.

## What you've got now
- **Background poller** hits Gmail's **History API** every 8s — it only returns *deltas*, so it's cheap (no full inbox refetch when nothing changed).
- When anything changes (new mail, archive, label change — from this app *or* from Gmail/your phone), it pushes an event over **SSE** (`/api/stream`) to the open tab, and the **inbox refreshes itself**.
- A small **green dot** in the app bar (next to Refresh) flashes when a sync lands, so you get visual confirmation it's live.
- Works across all views — inbox, bundles, Snoozed, Done, search all auto-update.

## Verified live
Captured the SSE stream while toggling a label: the poller caught the change, bumped the version, and the stream pushed `data: {"version": 1}` to the client within one poll cycle — with heartbeats holding the connection open. Reader/compose overlays are untouched by a refresh, so it won't interrupt you mid-read or mid-compose.

## Why SSE + History instead of "real" Gmail push
True Gmail push (`users().watch()` + Pub/Sub) requires Google to POST to a **public HTTPS endpoint** — a `127.0.0.1` app can't receive that without running a tunnel, which is brittle for a daily-driver email client. The SSE + History approach gives the same hands-off "it just updates" behavior with no external dependencies. If you ever want sub-second push and don't mind a tunnel, that's a clean future upgrade — but for a local client this is the right tradeoff.

One thing to be aware of: latency is up to ~8s (the poll interval) — effectively live for email. I can tighten that interval if you want it snappier, at the cost of slightly more API calls. README and memory are updated.

To test it yourself: send yourself an email (or have something arrive) and watch it appear in the open tab within a few seconds, without touching Refresh.

blocks.text:
Hell yes. Let me scope this precisely first, because "one-click unsubscribe" is a real spec, not just a button.

## How it actually works (and how Gmail does it)
Unsubscribe is driven by two email headers:
- **`List-Unsubscribe`** (RFC 2369): one or more URIs — a `mailto:` and/or an `https://` link.
- **`List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click`** (RFC 8058): the sender's signal that it supports *true* one-click — the client sends an HTTP **POST** to the https URI and you're unsubscribed with no landing page.

Gmail's logic, which I'll replicate exactly:
1. **One-Click** (RFC 8058 header present + https URI) → server-side `POST List-Unsubscribe=One-Click`. Silent, instant.
2. **mailto only** → send an unsubscribe email from your account (we have the `gmail.send` scope). Also silent.
3. **https link only** (no one-click) → open the page in a browser (can't safely auto-submit; the sender wants a human).

I'll re-read the headers server-side at action time (never trust a client-passed URL), surface it **inline on inbox cards** and **at the top of the open email**, but only when the header actually exists.

blocks.text:
One-click unsubscribe is built and verified (short of firing a real one, which is yours to click). Fresh tab is open.

## Scope, as implemented
It's the real spec, not a fake button — driven by the actual email headers, exactly like Gmail:

| Sender's headers | What the app does |
|---|---|
| `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` + https URI (RFC 8058) | Server `POST`s `List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` to the URI — silent, instant |
| `mailto:` only | Sends an unsubscribe email from your account |
| https link only (no one-click) | Opens the sender's page in a browser |

## Where it shows (only when a `List-Unsubscribe` header exists)
- **Inline in the inbox** — a small blue "Unsubscribe" link next to the sender name on the card.
- **At the top of the email** — a yellow banner with an Unsubscribe button when you open the thread.

## Verified
- **Detection on your real inbox:** 17 of 32 messages carry the header, all correctly classified as one-click (Patreon, Affirm, Nintendo, LinkedIn Job Alerts, …).
- **Endpoint:** live, re-reads headers server-side at click time (never trusts a client-passed URL), and fails gracefully on bad input.
- **Safety:** a confirmation prompt ("Unsubscribe from [sender]?") guards every click, and the server only auto-submits true one-click (https POST) or mailto — plain links open in the browser so a human completes them.

## Two deliberate choices
1. **I did not fire a live unsubscribe.** It's destructive and hard to undo, and several of your subscriptions (LinkedIn Job Alerts especially) matter during the job hunt. The action is ready for you to click when *you* decide.
2. The **confirm dialog** is intentional given the link sits right on the cards — it prevents an accidental click from quietly unsubscribing you.

Try it on something you genuinely want gone (a promo you don't care about) — you'll get the confirm prompt, then a "Unsubscribed ✓" / "Unsubscribe email sent" toast. README and memory are updated.

blocks.text:
Fixed and stress-tested. A fresh tab is open with the inbox restored.

## What actually broke
When I added live sync, I set the Flask server to `threaded=True` so SSE could hold a connection. But the Gmail client library sits on **`httplib2`, which is not thread-safe** — so the background history poller (every 8s) and your click handlers started using the *same* connection at the same time. That corrupts the connection: the in-flight call hangs ("Unsubscribing…"), then it times out ("operation timed out"), and every Gmail call after it 500s — which is why the whole inbox went blank. The unsubscribe was just the request unlucky enough to collide first.

## The fix
1. **Serialized all Gmail calls** behind a single lock (`API_LOCK`) — the poller and your requests now take turns instead of clobbering the shared connection. (The external unsubscribe POST to the sender stays *outside* the lock, so a slow sender can't freeze the app.)
2. **Added a 30s socket timeout** to the Gmail connection, so a genuinely stuck call now fails cleanly instead of hanging forever.
3. Restarted the server to clear the already-wedged connection.

## Verified
- Inbox loads again.
- **12 concurrent inbox requests → all 200.**
- Mixed concurrent load (inbox + thread + snoozed + done + search, all at once) → all 200.
- **Zero 500s** in the log after the fix.

## On "Olivia from Singa"
Looking at the logs, a couple of your earlier unsubscribe attempts *did* return 200 before the wedge, so Singa may already be unsubscribed. Just try it again now — it'll either complete cleanly ("Unsubscribed ✓") or, if you're already off their list, it'll just confirm. Either way the app won't lock up anymore.

Reload your tab if it still shows blank (it should already be fine in the new one). I've logged this thread-safety gotcha in memory so live-sync + Gmail concurrency doesn't bite again.

Fixed (v=9 is open).

**What was happening:** email bodies render inside a sandboxed iframe. When you clicked a link, the browser tried to load that site *inside the frame*, and most sites send `X-Frame-Options: DENY` to refuse being embedded — Chrome reports that as `ERR_BLOCKED_BY_RESPONSE`.

**The fix:** links in emails now open in a **new browser tab** as a normal top-level navigation (which sites allow), instead of loading inside the frame. Two changes:
- Injected `<base target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">` into the rendered email so every link defaults to opening in a new tab.
- Loosened the iframe sandbox just enough (`allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox`) so those links open as real, unsandboxed tabs.

Security is unchanged where it matters: the email still can't run JavaScript (no `allow-scripts`), so it's display-only — links just open outward in a fresh tab now.

Open an email and click a link — it should pop a new tab to the destination instead of erroring. Let me know if any link still misbehaves.

Done (v=10 is open).

## Your question answered
**The old limit was 60 messages per load** — and since they get grouped into threads and split across bundles, you saw even fewer at once. Archiving revealed the next 60 from the top, which is the behavior you noticed.

## What I changed
- **Raised the default to 100 messages/page** and added a **"Load more"** button at the bottom of the list. Each click pulls another 100 (up to 500/page).
- It applies everywhere — inbox, Snoozed, Done, and search results.
- **Live-sync keeps your depth:** if you've loaded 300, an auto-refresh re-loads all 300 (and keeps your expanded bundles + scroll position), so you won't get bumped back to a short list.

## The constraint I had to fix first
Gmail's batch API caps at ~100 sub-requests per call, so simply raising the number would have errored out. I now **chunk the metadata fetch into groups of 50**, which is what makes higher limits work at all. Verified: `limit=120` returns all 120 (59 threads) with no batch error.

## One tradeoff to know
The deeper you load, the heavier each live-sync refresh gets (loading 300 = 6 batched calls each refresh, ~a couple seconds, serialized behind the thread-safety lock from earlier). It's fine at 100–200; if you routinely want to work hundreds deep, the cleaner long-term approach is true incremental pagination with `pageToken` (load-more appends instead of re-fetching) — I can build that next if you find yourself going deep a lot. For now, "Load more" gets you as far as you need.

Scroll to the bottom of your inbox and you'll see **Load more** — give it a click and the older mail appends right in.

Multi-select is built (v=16 is open). Here's how it works:

**Selecting:**
- Hover over a card's **contact avatar** → it flips to an empty checkbox circle.
- Click it → the row highlights (light blue), the checkbox fills blue, and it **stays selected** even when you move the mouse away.
- Click again to deselect (or use the bar's ✕).

**Bulk-action bar:**
- As soon as ≥1 email is selected, a **darker-blue bar appears at the top** showing "N selected" with bulk actions: **Send to Things 3, Pin, Snooze, Done**, plus an ✕ to clear.
- **Done** archives all selected, **Pin** pins all, **Send to Things** creates a task per email (with the backlink), **Snooze** opens the preset menu and snoozes all selected at once.
- After any action, the selection clears and the inbox refreshes.

**Plus:** selection survives live-sync refreshes (selected rows stay checked when new mail arrives), and clicking the avatar won't open the thread or trigger a swipe.

A couple of notes:
- It updates the count live as you check more.
- I documented this in memory along with the rest of the app.

text: If we create a way to re-label emails, will that tune the algorithm at all, or just re-label that one email?

blocks.text:
Great question, and the answer is **just that one email** — as built, nothing learns from a re-label. But the "why" splits along the two categorization layers the app actually uses:

## The two layers
1. **Gmail's native categories** (Promos, Social, Updates, Forums) — assigned server-side by *Gmail's* classifier. Our app just reads those labels.
2. **Our keyword heuristic** (Travel, Purchases, Finance) — plain regex on subject/sender/snippet, computed fresh on every fetch. Not stored anywhere.

## What a re-label would actually do
- **Re-labeling a Gmail-category email** (e.g., move Promos → Primary via the API): that's a one-message label change. Gmail's classifier does **not** reliably retrain from a single edit — there's no learning signal you can drive through the API by editing one message. (Gmail's web UI sometimes asks "do this for future messages?" — but that's it quietly creating a *filter*, not retraining a model.)
- **Re-labeling a heuristic email** (Travel/Purchases/Finance): it wouldn't even persist. The bundle is recomputed by regex on the next load, so your change would vanish. And since it's static regex, there's no model to tune.

So neither path "tunes an algorithm" today.

## The real lever, if you want it to stick: Gmail filters
The practical way to make a re-label *teach* the system for future mail is **server-side Gmail filters** (rules), which the Gmail API fully supports (`users().settings().filters().create`). A filter like "from `marketing@store.com` → apply label X, skip Promos" deterministically routes all *future* matching mail. That's not ML, but it behaves like learning and it persists across devices because it lives in your Gmail account.

I could wire this up so re-labeling works like Gmail's "Do this for future messages from [sender]?" prompt:
- **One email** → just relabel that message.
- **Checkbox: "always do this for this sender"** → also create a Gmail filter so future mail lands where you want.

A lighter-weight alternative for *our* Travel/Purchases/Finance bundles specifically: keep a small local **sender→bundle override map** (in `snooze.db`) that the heuristic checks first — so correcting "this sender is Finance, not Promos" sticks for that sender going forward. That's rule-memory, not a trained model, but it's the honest, reliable version of "tuning."

**Bottom line:** true model retraining isn't on the table (Gmail's model isn't ours to train, and ours is regex). But filters (account-wide, future mail) and/or a local override map (our bundles) give you the same practical outcome. Want me to build the filter-based "apply to future from this sender" re-label, the local override map, or both?

text: Let's do the filter-based "apply to future emails from this sender" re-labeling.

blocks.text:

I'll walk you through that re-auth.
