Filter-based re-labeling is built, verified end-to-end, and live (v=18 is open, re-authed with the new scope).

## How to use it
- On any card (hover actions) or in an open email, click the **label icon** → a **"Move to bundle"** menu opens with all eight targets (Primary, Travel, Purchases, Finance, Promos, Social, Updates, Forums).
- Pick a bundle → that email moves there immediately.
- Check **"Apply to future from [sender]"** before picking → it *also* creates a Gmail filter so all future mail from that sender auto-lands in that bundle.

## How it works under the hood
- **The move** applies a `Bundle/<name>` Gmail label that **overrides** both the keyword heuristic and Gmail's native category — so it sticks and wins. (`Bundle/Primary` forces an email out of all bundles.)
- **"Apply to future"** creates a real **Gmail filter** (`from:sender → add Bundle/<name>`), which lives in your Gmail account, so it works across all your devices, not just this app. It de-dupes (won't create the same filter twice).

## Verified
- Re-labeling a `CATEGORY_PROMOTIONS` email to **Finance** correctly moved it (the override beat the native category), and it surfaced in the Finance bundle after Gmail's ~1-2s propagation.
- The **filter creation** path works (created → confirmed → deleted in testing).
- I cleaned up every test artifact (test filter + test label removed).

## Two notes
1. **The re-auth you just did is one-time** — the new `gmail.settings.basic` scope is saved, so it won't ask again.
2. There's a brief (~1-2s) lag after a move before Gmail reflects the label, so the bundle change may appear a moment after you pick it (the live-sync refresh guarantees it lands).

Auto-fill is wired and the data supports it: page 1 returns 50 messages → **39 threads** with a `nextPageToken`, so on load the client sees 39 < 50 and automatically pulls the next page to get back above 50.

Here's the behavior now:
- **On load**, the inbox auto-pages until **≥50 conversations** are in view (or there are no more).
- **As you triage** (Done, Snooze, etc.), when the visible count drops below 50, it silently pulls the next page to top it back up — so you always have a full screen to work through.
- It only applies to the **main inbox** view (not pinned-only, Snoozed/Done/search), and it stops cleanly once Gmail runs out of messages, so a near-empty inbox won't loop.
- The manual **Load more** button still works if you want to go deeper than 50.

Both features are in and serving (v=23 is open).

## Rich text (compose modal)
The compose body is now a formatting editor with a toolbar: **Bold**, *Italic*, Underline, and **Insert link** (anchor text — select text, click 🔗, enter a URL; bare domains get `https://` auto-prepended). Editing a saved draft pulls its HTML back in so formatting is preserved.

## Attachments
A **paperclip** button in the toolbar opens a file picker (multi-select). Attached files show as removable chips under the body, and they're uploaded with the message as real MIME attachments (`multipart/mixed`) via `FormData`.

text: Google Chrome is a RAM hog, is there any way for this app to be stand-alone, not a web app?

blocks.text:
Yes — and you don't have to live with Chrome's footprint. The key insight: Chrome is heavy because it's Chromium (hundreds of MB per window). The fix is to run the app in a **WebKit** surface instead (macOS's built-in engine, dramatically lighter), so the app keeps all its current code but stops living in Chrome.

There are a few ways to get there, with a real tradeoff between effort and how "standalone" it feels:

text: Which is lowest RAM usage, and are there any other tradeoffs?

blocks.text:
Good questions. Here's the honest picture.

## Lowest RAM
**pywebview and Safari-Add-to-Dock are roughly tied for lowest** — both render in macOS's system **WebKit**, which is far lighter than Chromium and shares frameworks already loaded by the OS. **Chrome "Install app" is the heaviest of the three** because it's still Chromium under the hood.

Rough, approximate footprints (they vary by machine/content):

| Option | Engine | Ballpark RAM | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **pywebview** | WebKit (WKWebView) | **~150–300 MB** total | Python server (~50MB) + one WebKit content process. Self-contained. |
| **Safari → Add to Dock** | WebKit | **~150–300 MB** | Similar, but split: the WebKit window **plus** the Flask server running separately. |
| **Chrome Install app** | Chromium | **~400 MB–1 GB+** | Browser + GPU + renderer processes; only modestly lighter than a normal Chrome window. |
| *(today) Chrome tab* | Chromium | highest | What you're trying to escape. |

So: **pywebview is the lowest** by a hair (most integrated, nothing else loaded), with Safari essentially equal on the rendering side. The real win in all cases is dropping Chromium.

## The other tradeoffs that actually matter

**pywebview (my recommendation)**
- ✅ True standalone app: one dock icon, starts its own server, no browser, deep links can focus *its* window.
- ⚠️ I have to build it; adds a Python dependency (pywebview + pyobjc).
- ⚠️ Two things I'd need to handle in the WebKit window: (1) **external links in emails** — WKWebView doesn't open new tabs on its own, so I'll route "open link" clicks to your default browser; (2) the **one-time Google consent** still opens your system browser (unavoidable, once).
- ⚠️ No browser conveniences (devtools, extensions, browser password autofill).

**Safari → Add to Dock**
- ✅ Zero code, ~30 seconds, you own it; auto-updates since it's just the page.
- ⚠️ **Two pieces:** the Flask server (Inbox.app) must be running separately, or the web app shows a connection error. Not fully self-contained.
- ⚠️ **Deep links are messier:** a Things `inboxclone://` link would still pop a browser tab rather than focusing the Safari web app — inconsistent with the rest.
- ⚠️ Requires macOS Sonoma+ (you're fine).

**Chrome Install app**
- ✅ Zero code; keeps Chrome's autofill/extensions/devtools.
- ⚠️ Still Chromium = smallest RAM win; mostly defeats the purpose.

## Bottom line
If your goal is **lowest RAM + a genuine standalone app with the deep links intact**, go **pywebview** — it's the cleanest fit and I'll handle the link-routing and deep-link focus. If you'd rather spend **zero effort right now** and accept that the server stays a separate piece and deep links open in a browser, **Safari Add to Dock** gets you ~the same RAM today with no code.

blocks.text: Now the desktop entry point (`desktop.py`) — runs the server in-process and shows it in a native WebKit window via pywebview:

blocks.name: Write

input.content:
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = [
#   "flask",
#   "google-api-python-client",
#   "google-auth-oauthlib",
#   "google-auth-httplib2",
#   "pywebview",
#   "pyobjc-framework-Cocoa",
#   "pyobjc-framework-WebKit",
# ]
# ///
"""
Inbox desktop shell — runs the Flask server in-process and renders it in a native
macOS WKWebView window (via pywebview). No Chromium, far less RAM than a browser.

Deep links (inboxclone://thread/<id>) are delivered by the separate AppleScript
scheme handler, which POSTs /api/open_thread; the SPA picks it up over SSE.
"""
import threading
import time
import urllib.request
import webbrowser

import webview
import app as inbox

URL = f"http://127.0.0.1:{inbox.PORT}/"


class Api:
    # Exposed to the page as window.pywebview.api.open_external(url)
    def open_external(self, url):
        try:
            webbrowser.open(url)
        except Exception:
            pass
        return True


def _server_up():
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(URL + "api/health", timeout=1)
        return True
    except Exception:
        return False


def main():
    # Singleton: if a server is already serving, don't start a second one.
    if _server_up():
        print("Inbox is already running.")
        return
    inbox.start_background()  # scheduler + auth (opens browser once on first run) + history poller
    threading.Thread(
        target=lambda: inbox.app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=inbox.PORT,
                                     debug=False, threaded=True, use_reloader=False),
        daemon=True,
    ).start()
    for _ in range(160):  # wait up to ~40s for the server to come up
        if _server_up():
            break
        time.sleep(0.25)
    webview.create_window("Inbox", URL, js_api=Api(),
                          width=1180, height=820, min_size=(820, 600))
    webview.start()  # blocks on the native GUI loop until the window closes


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

-- inboxclone:// scheme handler for the native (pywebview) Inbox app.
-- Ensures the desktop app is running, then asks its window to surface the thread
-- via POST /api/open_thread (the SPA picks it up over SSE). Falls back to Gmail.
property appPath : (POSIX path of (path to home folder)) & "Desktop/Apps/Inbox.app"
property serverURL : "http://127.0.0.1:5008"

on serverUp()
	try
		do shell script "curl -sf " & serverURL & "/api/health -o /dev/null"
		return true
	on error
		return false
	end try
end serverUp

on launchApp()
	do shell script "open " & quoted form of appPath
end launchApp

on run
	launchApp()
end run

on open location this_URL
	set threadId to ""
	set gmailURL to ""
	try
		set afterScheme to text ((offset of "thread/" in this_URL) + 7) thru -1 of this_URL
		if afterScheme contains "?" then
			set threadId to text 1 thru ((offset of "?" in afterScheme) - 1) of afterScheme
		else
			set threadId to afterScheme
		end if
	end try
	try
		if this_URL contains "gmail=" then
			set rawGmail to text ((offset of "gmail=" in this_URL) + 6) thru -1 of this_URL
			set gmailURL to do shell script "python3 -c 'import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.unquote(sys.argv[1]))' " & quoted form of rawGmail
		end if
	end try
	if not serverUp() then
		launchApp()
		repeat 120 times
			delay 0.5
			if serverUp() then exit repeat
		end repeat
	end if
	if serverUp() and threadId is not "" then
		do shell script "curl -s -X POST " & serverURL & "/api/open_thread -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d " & quoted form of ("{\"threadId\":\"" & threadId & "\"}")
		launchApp()
	else if gmailURL is not "" then
		do shell script "open " & quoted form of gmailURL
	end if
end open location

Done — Inbox is now a **standalone native app**, off Chrome entirely.

## What changed
- **`Inbox.app`** now opens in its own **macOS WebKit window** (WKWebView via pywebview) instead of a browser tab. It starts the server itself, has its own dock icon, and quitting the window shuts everything down. No Chromium.
- Verified live: the running app uses the system `com.apple.WebKit.WebContent`/`GPU`/`Networking` services — **not** Chromium.

## RAM (measured on your machine just now)
| | RAM |
|---|---|
| **Inbox native app** | ~250–350 MB (Python server ~187 MB + shared system WebKit) |
| **Chrome (current)** | 632 MB — and it grows per tab |

So roughly **half**, with the bonus that closing it frees everything cleanly (no lingering browser).

## The two things I had to handle (and did)
- **Email links** open in your default browser via a pywebview bridge — and I also fixed them to intercept cleanly (no more X-Frame errors), in both the native app and the browser fallback.
- **Things deep links** (`inboxclone://`) work via a tiny hidden helper app that tells the native window which thread to open (over SSE). Verified the scheme routes and the endpoint fires.

## How you use it now
- **Launch:** double-click **`~/Desktop/Apps/Inbox.app`** → native window.
- **First launch took ~84s** (one-time: `uv` downloaded pywebview + the macOS WebKit bindings). Subsequent launches are fast.
- **Browser still works** if you ever want it: `uv run --script app.py` then open localhost:5008.
- A hidden helper, **`Inbox Link Handler.app`**, now sits in your Apps folder — that's the deep-link router; you never open it directly.

The native window is open on your screen now. One honest note: the Python side (~187 MB) is the bulk of the footprint — lighter than Chrome but not tiny, since it's loading Flask + the Google libraries. If you ever want it leaner, the path would be a compiled/bundled build, but that's a bigger lift for modest gain. text: How much leaner could we get it? Rough estimate

blocks.text:
Rough numbers — here's where the ~250–350 MB actually goes, and what each lever buys you. (All approximate; RAM varies.)

## Where it's going now
| Piece | ~RAM | Reducible? |
|---|---|---|
| `uv run` wrapper process | ~40 MB | **Yes, easily** — pure overhead |
| Python + Flask + **google-api-python-client** + pyobjc | ~187 MB | Partially — the Google client is the hog |
| System WebKit (WebContent/GPU/Networking) | ~50–110 MB (mostly shared) | Mostly no — it's the cost of rendering HTML |

## What you could shave, by effort

**Tier A — quick wins (~30 min): → ~210–280 MB**
- Drop the `uv run` parent by exec'ing a prebuilt venv's Python directly: **~40 MB** back.
- Minor trims. Low risk, keeps everything as-is.

**Tier B — replace `google-api-python-client` with raw Gmail REST (a few hours): → ~170–220 MB**
- That library + its Gmail "discovery document" is the single biggest chunk (~60–100 MB). Swapping to plain HTTPS calls + `google-auth` only (just for the token) cuts a meaningful **~40–70 MB**. Moderate rewrite of the backend calls, but the logic is the same.
- This is the best effort-to-payoff if you want it leaner without changing the architecture.

**Tier C — full native rewrite (Swift/SwiftUI + WKWebView, no Python): → ~80–150 MB**
- Eliminates the Python process entirely; you're left with a thin native shell + the WebKit content process (which is the floor for showing HTML). But it means rewriting *all* the Gmail/triage logic in Swift. High effort, and you'd lose the easy Python iteration we've been doing.

**Tier D — native UI with no web view at all: → ~40–80 MB**
- The theoretical floor. Requires rebuilding the entire interface in SwiftUI (no HTML/CSS/JS). Essentially a different product. Not worth it for a personal app.

## The honest takeaway
- The **WebContent process (~50–80 MB) is a hard floor** for anything that renders our HTML UI — you can't get under that without abandoning the web stack (Tier C/D).
- Realistic sweet spot staying on this codebase: **Tier A gets you to ~250 MB for ~30 min of work; A+B to ~180–220 MB for a few hours.** That's ~3–3.5× lighter than Chrome's 632 MB.
- Going below ~180 MB means leaving Python behind — large effort, modest absolute gain.

My recommendation: **Tier A is a no-brainer** if you want a quick ~40 MB. **Tier B** only if the footprint genuinely bugs you day-to-day. Below that isn't worth the rewrite. Want me to do Tier A (and/or B)?

Both write and read paths work through the new REST client. Done — here are the numbers.

## Results (measured on your machine, same window)

| | Before (uv + google-api-client) | After (venv + raw REST) |
|---|---|---|
| Process tree | `uv → python` (extra ~43 MB wrapper) | just `python desktop.py` |
| Python process | 187 MB | **169 MB** |
| `uv` wrapper | ~43 MB | **gone** |
| **Total (app + WebKit)** | ~353 MB | **~276 MB** |
| Startup | 84s first run | **~4s** |

So **~77 MB lighter (~22%)**, and now **~2.3× lighter than Chrome** (632 MB). Everything still works — verified inbox load, thread fetch, drafts, and a pin/unpin write round-trip all go through the new raw-HTTPS Gmail client.

## Honest breakdown of where the savings came from
- **Tier A (drop the `uv` wrapper): ~43 MB** — the bigger, cleaner win. The app now runs from a prebuilt `.venv` directly.
- **Tier B (raw Gmail REST instead of `google-api-python-client`): ~18 MB** on the Python side — less than my high estimate. The discovery-client wasn't as heavy as feared; the remaining 169 MB is mostly the **pyobjc/pywebview** native bindings, which are the floor for a WebKit window.

So we got most of the realistic gain. To go meaningfully lower (~80–150 MB) you'd have to drop Python entirely (Tier C native rewrite) — not worth it.

## What changed structurally
- `app.py` now talks to Gmail over plain HTTPS via google-auth's `AuthorizedSession` (thread-safe, so I removed the old global lock; metadata fetches now run concurrently via a thread pool instead of batch requests).
- Dependencies dropped: `google-api-python-client`, `google-auth-httplib2`, `httplib2`. Kept: `google-auth`, `google-auth-oauthlib`, `requests`.
- `Inbox.app` launches `./.venv/bin/python desktop.py` — no `uv` at runtime.

text: Remind me why a full rewrite in SwiftUI wouldn't be worth it?

blocks.text:
Sure — here's the recap, now that you've actually seen the numbers.

## 1. The RAM you'd save is small in absolute terms
You're at **~276 MB**. A SwiftUI rewrite lands at:
- **Tier C** (Swift shell + WKWebView, reuse the web UI): ~80–150 MB
- **Tier D** (full native SwiftUI views, no web): ~40–80 MB

So you'd reclaim ~130–230 MB. On a normal Mac that's noise — and the thing you set out to kill (Chrome at 632 MB) is *already* gone. The 632→276 win was the real prize; this would be chasing a rounding error.

## 2. It's a total rewrite of everything we built
All of this currently lives in Python + HTML/JS and would have to be re-implemented in Swift from scratch: the Gmail REST client, OAuth + token handling, bundles, the SQLite snooze store **and its background scheduler**, highlights, RFC-8058 unsubscribe, the re-label **Gmail filters**, multi-select, drafts, **rich-text compose + MIME attachments**, **live sync over SSE**, and the **Things deep-link** integration. That's weeks of work to reproduce features that already work today.

## 3. You'd lose the iteration speed that made all this possible
The reason we added ~a dozen features quickly is the edit-a-file-and-restart loop of Python + web. Swift means Xcode, compile cycles, code signing, and more ceremony — every future tweak gets slower. You've been changing this thing daily; that gets painful.

## 4. The big floor doesn't move (Tier C)
If you keep the web UI in a Swift WKWebView shell, you **still pay the same WebKit content process** (~50–80 MB) we already use. The only thing Tier C sheds is the ~169 MB Python process — by rewriting the entire backend in Swift. Enormous effort to delete one process.

## 5. Tier D throws away the actual product
Getting to ~40–80 MB means dropping HTML/CSS/JS and rebuilding the UI in native SwiftUI views — which discards the design-spec-faithful Inbox recreation (the exact Material look, the toolbar, contenteditable rich text). You'd be re-drawing the whole interface in a different paradigm.

## 6. You'd lose portability
Today it's "Python + a browser" — the browser fallback runs on any OS, any machine. A SwiftUI app is macOS-only and Apple-locked, with no escape hatch.

## When it *would* be worth it
- You want to ship it to other people as a polished Mac App Store product.
- You want deep native integration (menu-bar app, native notifications, Handoff).
- Sub-100 MB is a hard constraint on a very memory-starved machine.

None of those apply to a personal daily-driver on a normal Mac. **Bottom line:** you already fixed the problem you had (Chrome's footprint). A SwiftUI rewrite is large, slow, and lossy for a gain you won't feel — classic diminishing returns.

blocks.text:
Fixed and confirmed stable. Over 18 seconds the window now does exactly one initial load + one auto-fill page (and then sits quietly — no reset loop), so it lands at **~83 in view** (page 1's 37 threads + page 2's 46), comfortably past your 50.

## What was actually wrong
Not the logic — the **WKWebView was running a stale cached copy of the JavaScript**. The auto-fill code was correct (the server-side paging proves it: page 2 adds 46 new threads), but the window kept executing an old `app.js` that didn't run the fill, so it stopped at page 1 (37).

## The fix (two parts, so it can't recur)
1. **Bumped the asset version** → forced the window to load current JS. Auto-fill immediately kicked in (the `pageToken` request now appears in the log).
2. **Added `Cache-Control: no-cache` on static files** (verified in the response headers) so the webview always revalidates — future JS changes take effect on relaunch instead of getting silently cached.

I also added a `desktop.log` so the app's requests are observable now (it launches detached, so there was no log before — that's why I'd been looking at a stale `server.log` from an old browser session).

The app is running the fresh build now and showing the filled inbox. One note: because each page is 50 *messages* (which collapse to ~37–46 threads), the fill overshoots 50 to ~80 in one step — that's "at least 50," as intended; it can't land exactly on 50 without fetching partial pages.

I restarted the app a few times while diagnosing — apologies for the churn. It's stable now; the window you have open is the fixed build.

def thread_summary(msg, outgoing=False):
    """Build a list-row summary from a metadata message resource.
    outgoing=True (Sent) shows the recipient ('To: …') instead of the sender."""
    headers = msg.get("payload", {}).get("headers", [])
    subject = _header(headers, "Subject") or "(no subject)"
    labels = msg.get("labelIds", [])
    snippet = msg.get("snippet", "")
    if outgoing:
        name, addr = _parse_addr(_header(headers, "To"))
        sender = "To: " + (name or "(no recipient)")
        bundle = None
    else:
        name, addr = _parse_addr(_header(headers, "From"))
        sender = name
        bundle = _bundle_for(labels, subject, name, snippet)
    return {
        "id": msg.get("threadId"),

def summarize_ids(ids):
    if not ids:
        return []
    load_bundle_labels()
    headers = ["From", "Subject", "Date", "List-Unsubscribe", "List-Unsubscribe-Post"]
    # Concurrent metadata fetches (requests/urllib3 is thread-safe). gget retries
    # rate-limits internally; a small worker cap keeps us under the per-second quota.
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as ex:
        msgs = list(ex.map(lambda m: _get_meta(m, headers), ids))

    # newest message per thread
    by_thread = {}
    for msg in msgs:
        if not msg:
            continue
        tid = msg.get("threadId")
        prev = by_thread.get(tid)
        if not prev or int(msg.get("internalDate", 0)) > int(prev.get("internalDate", 0)):
            by_thread[tid] = msg
    summaries = [thread_summary(m) for m in by_thread.values()]
    summaries.sort(key=lambda r: int(r["ts"]), reverse=True)
    return summaries

Genuinely happy to get this on your iPhone — but there's a big fork here, and the right path depends on a tradeoff only you can call. The core issue: **your app has a Python server (Flask) that talks to Gmail. An iPhone can't run that Python server itself**, so the question is whether to keep the server on your Mac (cheap, but the Mac has to be on) or rewrite to remove it (lots of work, but truly standalone).

One thing up front that applies to all paths: putting a Gmail-connected server on a network the phone can reach has a **security angle** (right now it only listens on the Mac itself). I'd handle that with a private network (Tailscale) or an access token rather than exposing it on open WiFi.

Here are the realistic options:

What would you like to clarify before you pick? Happy to dig into any of it. A few things I can expand on:

- **How "always on" your Mac realistically is** — this is the big decider. If your Mac is a desktop/mini that stays on, the Mac-served option is basically all upside. If it's a laptop that sleeps/travels with you, that option gets frustrating away from home.
- **What "use it on my iPhone" means for you** — mostly at home/on your own WiFi, or genuinely on the go (commute, travel) with the Mac potentially asleep?
- **What Tailscale is / what setup it needs** — it's a free private-network app that lets your iPhone reach your Mac securely from anywhere, without exposing anything to the open internet. ~5 min to set up on both devices.
- **Which features you actually care about on mobile** — e.g., if you mostly want to read/triage/compose, the standalone PWA's degraded bits (the background snooze scheduler, one-click unsubscribe) might not matter to you, which could change my recommendation.
- **The native-app reality** — the 7-day expiry on a free Apple ID means re-plugging into your Mac and re-installing weekly; the $99/yr account removes that. And it's weeks of rebuilding everything in Swift.
- **A hybrid I didn't list** — a native shell that bundles the web UI on the phone but still needs a Gmail backend somewhere.

What's on your mind — and roughly, is your Mac usually on and reachable, or do you need this to work with the Mac off?

Good — Mac-independence rules out option 1, so it's PWA vs native. Here's the honest difference:

## What each one *is*
- **Option 2 (PWA):** your existing HTML/CSS/JS UI, **hosted as static files on free always-on hosting (e.g., GitHub Pages)**, with the backend logic rewritten into browser JavaScript so the phone talks to Gmail directly. You "Add to Home Screen" → real icon, fullscreen. The Mac is gone *and* there's no server to run — GitHub Pages just serves the static files; your phone does everything else.
- **Option 3 (native):** a from-scratch **SwiftUI** app. The Inbox UI we built (HTML/CSS) gets thrown away and re-drawn in Swift; the Gmail logic gets rewritten in Swift too.

## How they compare

| | **Option 2 — PWA** | **Option 3 — Native** |
|---|---|---|
| Effort | **Days** (reuse the UI; rewrite backend→JS) | **Weeks** (rebuild *everything* in Swift) |
| Reuses our work | ✅ the whole UI | ❌ starts over |
| Install | Safari → Add to Home Screen | Xcode sideload |
| Apple account | **None** | Free ID → **re-install every 7 days**; or $99/yr |
| Needs Mac at all | No (host on GitHub Pages) | **Yes, to build/re-sign** the app |
| Expires | Never | Free tier: weekly |
| Iteration speed | Fast (edit + push) | Slow (Xcode builds) |

## The catch with Option 2 — a few features degrade
Because it runs in the browser sandbox with no server:
- **Snooze scheduler** — can't re-file mail to your inbox in the background while the app is closed. It'd only "wake" snoozed mail when you open the app (or I'd add a tiny free serverless cron to handle it).
- **One-click unsubscribe** — the silent POST to the sender is blocked by browser CORS, so it degrades to "open the unsubscribe page." (mailto-unsubscribe still works.)
- **Notifications** — limited (iOS web push is finicky).
- Everything else — read/triage/bundles/search/compose+attachments/drafts/sent/live-sync/**Send-to-Things** (Things is on iOS) — works.

Option 3 has none of those limits (full background, real notifications, native unsubscribe) — that's what the weeks of Swift buy you.

## One small setup note either way
Both need a new Google OAuth client (Option 2 → "Web application" type tied to your GitHub Pages URL; Option 3 → "iOS" type). ~5 minutes.

## My recommendation
For *personal, Mac-independent, real-app-on-the-home-screen* — **Option 2 (PWA)** is the clear winner: days not weeks, reuses the UI we built, no Apple account, no weekly expiry, free hosting, works anywhere. The only real loss is background snooze, which I can patch with a tiny free serverless cron if you use snooze a lot.

Native only wins if you specifically need flawless background behavior and native polish, and you're OK with weeks of work plus the build/re-sign friction.

Want me to go with **Option 2**? If so, tell me whether you lean on **snooze** much (decides whether I add the little serverless piece), and I'll lay out the steps.

# Roadmap

## ⏳ iPhone app — standalone PWA (deferred)

**Goal:** use this on iPhone as a real home-screen app, **independent of the Mac**
(Mac may be off). Decided direction: **client-side PWA** (not a native SwiftUI rewrite —
weeks of work, Xcode sideload, 7-day expiry on a free Apple ID).

### Plan (Option 2)
- **Host the frontend as static files on free always-on HTTPS** (e.g., GitHub Pages /
  Cloudflare Pages). No server to run.
- **Move the backend (`app.py`) logic into browser JavaScript** — talk to the Gmail REST
  API directly with `fetch`. OAuth via **Google Identity Services** (token client / PKCE).
- **New Google OAuth client of type "Web application"**, with the Pages URL as an
  authorized JS origin (the current one is a Desktop client).
- **Make the UI responsive** for phone (drawer becomes an overlay, full-width cards,
  app bar fits a narrow screen). Add a **web app manifest** + apple-touch-icon so
  "Add to Home Screen" gives an icon + fullscreen standalone mode.

### What carries over for free
Read / triage / bundles / pin / done / search / compose + attachments / drafts / sent /
live-sync (SSE) / **Send-to-Things** (Things has an iOS URL scheme).

### Known degradations to handle (browser sandbox, no server)
- **Snooze scheduler** — no background execution; snoozed mail can't re-file itself while
  the app is closed. Options: (a) re-file on app open + periodic foreground check, or
  (b) a tiny free serverless cron (Cloudflare Worker) that re-adds `INBOX` at wake time.
- **One-click unsubscribe** — the silent POST to the sender is blocked by browser CORS;
  degrades to "open the unsubscribe page." (mailto-unsubscribe still works via Gmail send.)
- **Notifications** — iOS web push (16.4+) is possible but finicky; likely skip initially.

### Rough effort
Days (reuses the existing HTML/CSS/JS UI; the work is OAuth-in-browser + porting Gmail
calls to client-side `fetch` + responsive CSS + manifest).

### Alternative considered (rejected for now)
- **Native SwiftUI app** — most polished + full background/notifications, but a from-scratch
  Swift rewrite (weeks), needs a Mac to build/re-sign, and free-Apple-ID builds expire
  every 7 days. Revisit only if background snooze/notifications become must-haves.

blocks.text:
Honest answer: **there's no real difference right now — the Reminder button is a stub.** Both fan-out buttons call the same `openCompose()`; "Reminder" just additionally pre-fills the Subject field with the word "Reminder." So clicking either one opens the same New-message email composer.

```js
fabCompose  → openCompose()                       // empty email
fabReminder → openCompose({ subject: "Reminder" }) // same composer, subject pre-filled
```

**What it was *supposed* to be** (in the real Google Inbox, and in our design spec): a **Reminder is not an email**. It's a to-do you set for *yourself* that appears as a first-class card in your inbox — pinnable, snoozable, markable-done like a message, but with no recipient and nothing sent. (Inbox even auto-enriched them with "Assists," e.g. a business's phone number.)

I never built that as a distinct feature — it was on the "not yet built" list — so the FAB option is a leftover placeholder, which is why it's confusing.

**Options to make it actually mean something** (pick any):
1. **Remove the Reminder button** — simplest; the FAB just composes. No more confusion.
2. **Reminder → a Things 3 task** — fits how you already work (we have the Things integration). Clicking Reminder pops a quick "what do you need to do?" and creates a Things task. Arguably the most useful version for you.
3. **Reminder → email-to-self** — sends a short note to your own address so it lands back in your inbox as a reminder. Reuses the send path; keeps it "in the inbox" like the original.
4. **Build real in-app reminders** — first-class reminder cards in the inbox (own Gmail label, pin/snooze/done). Closest to the original, but the most work, and Gmail has no native "reminder" object so it'd be app-managed.

My suggestion: **#2 (Things 3 task)** — it's genuinely useful, matches your toolchain, and is quick. Want me to wire that up, or just remove the button?

Fixed and pushed (v=31). Incoming attachments now show up.

## What was wrong
The reader decoded the message body (text/HTML) but **never walked the MIME tree for attachment parts**, so files people sent you were silently dropped.

## What I added
- **Backend** parses each message's attachments (filename, type, size, Gmail attachment ID).
- **`/api/attachment/<msg>/<id>`** streams the decoded file with the right filename and content type — **previews images/PDFs inline**, downloads everything else.
- **Reader UI** now shows an **attachment chip** per file (📎 name + size) under each message; clicking it opens/downloads via your browser.

## Verified
On a real email in your inbox: it found `invite.ics` (4,714 bytes), and the download endpoint returned the exact file with proper headers. The app reloaded on the fresh build, so open any email with an attachment and you'll see the chips.

## One related limitation (different thing)
**Inline images** embedded in an email body (referenced as `cid:` inside the HTML) still won't render — that requires rewriting those references to fetch the image data, which is a separate piece. True file attachments (PDFs, docs, .ics, images sent as attachments, etc.) now work. If you're seeing broken inline images specifically, tell me and I'll wire that up too.

blocks.text:
Done and pushed (v=32). Attachments now appear right **on the inbox cards** — verified live: calendar invites, a PDF ("About TRM Labs.pdf"), etc. show as chips under the snippet.

## Behavior
- **Click a file chip → it downloads** (via `/api/attachment`, opening in your browser; images/PDFs preview inline).
- **Google Docs → open in Drive:** attachments with a Google-Apps type are flagged and routed to Google Drive instead of attempting a download.
- Chips work on both **cards and inside the reader**, and clicking one won't accidentally open the thread or trigger a swipe.

## How I made it cheap
The cards are built from a lightweight fetch that — I confirmed — **doesn't include attachment data**; only a `full` fetch does. So I switched the list fetch to `full` **with a `fields` mask** that returns the headers + attachment structure but **excludes the email body bytes**. That gets attachments onto cards without downloading every message body. I also filter out **inline images** (logos/signatures) so promo emails don't show fake "attachments."

## Two honest notes
1. **Slight speed cost:** a 50-message page now takes ~2s (vs sub-second before) because it pulls the part tree. Still fine, but noticeable on load/refresh. If it bugs you, I can make the attachment enrichment lazy.
2. **The "Google Docs → Drive" path is best-effort.** Real Google Docs are usually *shared as Drive links in the email body*, not as MIME attachments — those links already open in Drive when you open the email (the reader routes links to your browser). The card-chip Drive handling only triggers if a message actually carries a Google-Apps *attachment part*, which is uncommon. If you have a specific email where a Google Doc isn't opening the way you want, forward me what it looks like and I'll tune it.
